questions.title: dbt Incremental Strategies: append, merge, and delete+insert
questions.prompt: A teammate's dbt model is materialized as incremental but keeps producing duplicate rows after reruns. Explain the difference between dbt's append, merge, and delete+insert incremental strategies, and which one actually prevents duplicates when a batch can be reprocessed.
questions.modelAnswer: The append strategy simply inserts every row that passes the is_incremental() filter with no deduplication at all -- if the same batch is reprocessed (a backfill run twice, a late retry), every row from that batch is inserted again, producing exact duplicates. The merge strategy requires a unique_key and performs an actual upsert (a MERGE INTO or engine-equivalent): rows matching an existing unique_key are updated in place, and only genuinely new keys are inserted, which makes reprocessing the same batch safe -- rerunning it updates the same rows to the same values rather than duplicating them. The delete+insert strategy also needs a key (often paired with a partition predicate): it first deletes every row matching the incoming batch's key/partition, then inserts the fresh rows -- functionally similar to merge for idempotency, but implemented as two statements instead of one atomic MERGE, and it's the strategy of choice on warehouses that don't support a native MERGE or when you specifically want to replace an entire partition's contents rather than row-by-row matching. Of the three, only merge and delete+insert are actually safe against reprocessing; append is not, by design, because it has no matching logic at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd ask first whether the model even has a unique_key set, because that's almost always the real story behind this exact symptom. Without unique_key, dbt's incremental model effectively just appends whatever passes the is_incremental() filter -- there's no concept of 'this row already exists' baked in, so running the same batch twice duplicates it every time. Once unique_key is set, I'd pick merge for most upsert-style loads because it's one atomic statement that updates matches and inserts new rows together. I'd reach for delete+insert specifically when I want to replace a whole partition's worth of data cleanly -- for example, reprocessing an entire day because an upstream bug affected it -- rather than relying on row-level matching, or when the warehouse adapter doesn't support merge well. Either way, the fix for duplicate rows is almost never 'rerun it less' -- it's making sure the model is actually keyed correctly for reprocessing in the first place.
commonMistakes: Setting materialized='incremental' without a unique_key and expecting duplicates to be prevented automatically
Assuming the append strategy is idempotent when it has no deduplication logic at all
Using merge without verifying unique_key actually matches the model's real grain (a single column when the grain is really composite)
Choosing delete+insert without defining the correct partition/delete boundary, so a rerun deletes more or less data than intended
keyPoints: Append strategy inserts every filtered row with no deduplication, so reruns duplicate data
Merge requires a unique_key and performs an atomic upsert, making reruns safe
Delete+insert deletes matching rows/partitions first, then inserts fresh data -- also safe for reruns
Delete+insert suits full-partition replacement or warehouses without native MERGE support
The unique_key (or delete predicate) must match the model's actual grain for the strategy to work correctly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains append's lack of deduplication
Correctly explains merge's upsert mechanics via unique_key
Correctly explains delete+insert's partition-replace use case
Identifies which strategies actually prevent duplicates on reprocessing

questions.title: The is_incremental() Macro and the Boundary Condition Trap
questions.prompt: Explain what the is_incremental() macro actually does in a dbt model, and describe the classic bug where an incremental filter's boundary condition (like event_time > max(event_time)) silently drops legitimate late-arriving rows.
questions.modelAnswer: is_incremental() returns true only when three conditions all hold: the target model already exists as a table in the warehouse, the run is not a --full-refresh, and the model is materialized as incremental -- on the very first run (or any full-refresh), it returns false so the whole source is processed unfiltered. It's used to wrap a WHERE clause that should only apply on subsequent incremental runs, typically filtering the source down to rows newer than what's already loaded. The classic bug shows up in exactly that filter: a boundary like WHERE event_time > (SELECT MAX(event_time) FROM {{ this }}) looks correct, but if a row arrives late -- its event_time is from two days ago, yet it only reaches the source table today because of upstream delay -- that boundary condition compares against the already-loaded max, which is newer than this late row's timestamp, so the row is filtered out and never loaded, permanently, with no error raised anywhere. The practical fix is to use a lookback window instead of a strict boundary (max(event_time) minus a few days) so recently-loaded data is re-scanned and late arrivals get picked up, combined with a unique_key merge so reprocessing already-loaded rows in that window doesn't create duplicates.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I always check first when someone reports 'missing rows that should be there' in an incremental model is the exact shape of the is_incremental() filter. A strict max(event_time) boundary assumes data always arrives in the order it was generated, which is rarely true in practice -- queues back up, retries happen, mobile clients sync hours later. Any of that produces a row whose event_time is older than what's already been loaded, and a strict greater-than filter will silently skip it forever, with the model looking perfectly healthy because nothing errored. I build a lookback window into basically every incremental filter I write now -- something like max(event_time) minus three days -- so the model re-scans a buffer of recently loaded data on every run. That only works safely combined with a merge strategy and the right unique_key, otherwise I'd just be creating duplicates of rows I already loaded instead of safely re-checking them.
commonMistakes: Using a strict greater-than boundary with no lookback window
Filtering on event-generation time instead of ingestion/load time when the source can arrive out of order
Forgetting is_incremental() returns false on the very first run, so the model's logic must also be correct unfiltered
Assuming a unique_key merge strategy alone fixes a filter that already excluded the late row before it reached the model
keyPoints: is_incremental() is true only when the table exists, it's not a full-refresh, and the model is incremental
A strict boundary filter silently drops rows that arrive later than data already loaded
A lookback window re-scans a buffer of recent data so late arrivals get picked up
Filtering on ingestion/load time instead of event time avoids this trap for genuinely out-of-order sources
A merge strategy with the correct unique_key is required for the lookback window to be safely re-processed without duplication

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains when is_incremental() returns true/false
Correctly explains the strict-boundary late-arrival bug
Describes the lookback-window fix and its dependency on a merge strategy
Distinguishes event-time from ingestion-time filtering

questions.title: Logical Date vs. Actual Run Time: Airflow's Scheduling Trap
questions.prompt: A DAG scheduled daily at midnight is supposed to process 'yesterday's data,' but a new engineer wires a task to use datetime.now() and gets wrong results on backfills. Explain Airflow's logical_date (data interval) concept and why DAG logic should reference it instead of wall-clock time.
questions.modelAnswer: Airflow schedules a run at the end of the interval it covers, not the start -- a DAG with schedule=@daily whose run is meant to cover January 1st actually fires at midnight on January 2nd, and the context Airflow hands that run carries logical_date (data_interval_start/data_interval_end in modern Airflow) equal to January 1st, not the moment it actually executed. Using datetime.now() inside task logic ties the DAG's behavior to the literal wall-clock moment the task happens to run, which breaks two things specifically: backfills, where many historical runs execute back-to-back at roughly the same real time but are each supposed to process a different historical date, and retries, where a task that fails and retries hours later would compute a completely different 'now' than the original attempt intended. The correct pattern is to use the templated context -- ds, logical_date, or data_interval_start/end via Jinja macros or the TaskFlow context -- to build date-scoped filenames, partition filters, or WHERE clauses, so a backfilled run for March 3rd always and only processes March 3rd's data, regardless of when it actually executes in real time.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it with the backfill example because that's where the bug becomes undeniable. If someone backfills the last 30 days and every task calls datetime.now(), every single one of those 30 runs computes essentially the same 'now,' even though they're each supposed to represent a different historical day -- the backfill becomes useless or actively wrong. The fix is always to template the date instead of computing it live: {{ ds }} for a string date, or the data_interval_start/end macros for a proper range. I treat 'does this DAG logic depend only on logical_date and never on wall-clock time' as a non-negotiable review check, because it's the single thing that makes a DAG safely re-runnable and backfillable, which is most of the point of using Airflow in the first place.
commonMistakes: Using datetime.now() or datetime.today() inside task logic instead of the templated logical date
Confusing logical_date with 'the actual time the DAG ran,' when it represents the data interval instead
Not understanding that @daily's interval covers [logical_date, logical_date + 1 day), not a single instant
Assuming backfills will 'just work' without checking that every task's logic is driven by the templated date
keyPoints: Airflow schedules a run at the end of the data interval it covers, not the start
logical_date (data_interval_start/end) represents the data being processed, not the real execution time
Using wall-clock time inside task logic breaks backfills, since every backfilled run would compute the same real time
Retries are also broken by wall-clock logic, since a retry hours later would compute a different 'now' than the original attempt
Templated macros (ds, logical_date, data_interval_start/end) should drive any date-scoped filtering or file naming

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains that logical_date represents the data interval, not execution time
Correctly explains the backfill failure mode from wall-clock logic
Correctly explains the retry failure mode from wall-clock logic
Names the correct templated macros/context to use instead

questions.title: Kafka's Ordering Guarantee Is Per-Partition Only
questions.prompt: A downstream consumer assumes messages arrive in the exact order they were produced across an entire Kafka topic. Explain why that assumption is wrong, and what actually determines ordering guarantees in Kafka.
questions.modelAnswer: Kafka guarantees ordering only within a single partition: messages appended to one partition are written and consumed in that exact sequence, because a partition is a single append-only log read by exactly one active consumer per consumer group at a time. A topic with multiple partitions has no guarantee at all about ordering across partitions, because each partition is an independent log that can be produced to and consumed from concurrently and at different rates. If strict ordering matters for a given logical entity -- all events for a specific customer_id must be processed in the order they happened -- the producer has to key each message so that every message for that entity hashes to the same partition (Kafka's default partitioner does this automatically from the key), guaranteeing those specific messages land in one ordered log even though the topic as a whole has no global order. The tradeoff is real: a single partition gives global order at the cost of all parallelism, while many partitions give parallelism at the cost of only being able to promise order within each key's partition, never across keys or across the topic.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd correct the assumption directly: Kafka never promised topic-wide order, only per-partition order, and that's a deliberate design tradeoff, not a missing feature. If a consumer needs strict ordering for a specific entity, the fix isn't at the consumer -- it's making sure the producer keys messages so that entity's events always land on the same partition, which the default partitioner handles automatically from the message key. What catches people off guard is that changing the partition count on an existing topic can change which partition a given key hashes to going forward, so an entity's historical events and its future events could end up split across different partitions after a repartition -- that's one more reason partition count isn't something to casually resize on a topic where per-key ordering actually matters.
commonMistakes: Assuming ordering holds across the whole topic rather than only within a partition
Keying messages inconsistently, so the same logical entity's events land on different partitions over time
Not realizing that increasing a topic's partition count changes future key-to-partition hashing
Conflating 'replayable in offset order within a partition' with a global ordering guarantee across the topic
keyPoints: Kafka guarantees order within a single partition only, never across the whole topic
A message's key determines which partition it lands on via the default partitioner's hashing
Strict per-entity ordering requires keying so that entity's messages always hash to the same partition
A single-partition topic gives full global order at the cost of all parallelism
Increasing partition count on an existing topic can change future key-to-partition assignment

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the per-partition-only ordering guarantee
Correctly explains how keying determines partition placement for ordering
Explains the parallelism-vs-ordering tradeoff
Mentions the repartition/key-hashing consequence

questions.title: Idempotent Producers, acks=all, and the Gap Between Them
questions.prompt: Explain what enable.idempotence=true actually prevents in a Kafka producer, what acks=all guarantees separately, and why having both still doesn't give you full end-to-end exactly-once delivery without more work on the consumer side.
questions.modelAnswer: enable.idempotence=true prevents duplicate messages caused specifically by producer-side retries: each producer is assigned a producer ID and tracks a per-partition sequence number, so if a network blip causes a retry of a message the broker already committed, the broker recognizes the duplicate sequence number and discards the resend rather than writing it twice -- this gives exactly-once writes from that specific producer into that specific partition. acks=all is a separate, durability-focused setting: it requires the partition leader to wait for acknowledgment from every in-sync replica before confirming the write back to the producer, which protects against data loss if the leader fails immediately after acknowledging but before replicas caught up. Combined, these two settings give you durable, non-duplicated delivery from producer to broker -- but that is not the same as end-to-end exactly-once. The gap is entirely on the consumer side: if a consumer processes a message, updates some downstream state, and then crashes before committing its offset, restarting will cause it to re-read and reprocess that same message -- a duplicate from the consumer's point of view that neither idempotent producers nor acks=all can prevent, because both only govern the producer-to-broker leg. True end-to-end exactly-once requires the consumer's processing and offset commit to be atomic with each other (writing both in the same transaction, or designing the downstream write itself to be idempotent), or using Kafka's transactional APIs to coordinate across the full read-process-write cycle.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd be specific that these two settings solve two different problems and neither one touches the consumer side at all. Idempotent producers stop a flaky network from turning one logical send into two physical writes. acks=all stops a leader failure from silently losing an acknowledged write. Put together, they make the producer-to-broker leg about as solid as it can be. But I've seen people treat 'enable.idempotence=true, acks=all' as a checkbox for 'we have exactly-once' and then get surprised when a consumer crash after processing but before committing its offset causes a visible duplicate downstream. That failure mode is entirely a consumer-side problem, and fixing it means either making whatever the consumer writes downstream naturally idempotent (an upsert on a natural key, for instance) or using Kafka transactions to tie the consume-process-produce cycle together atomically.
commonMistakes: Assuming enable.idempotence alone delivers full end-to-end exactly-once semantics
Conflating acks=all (durability) with deduplication, which it doesn't provide
Forgetting that a consumer crash after processing but before committing its offset is a duplicate source entirely outside producer configuration
Not using Kafka transactions or idempotent downstream writes when true end-to-end exactly-once is actually required
keyPoints: Idempotent producers deduplicate retried sends per partition using a producer ID and sequence number
acks=all is a durability guarantee (all in-sync replicas acknowledge), not a deduplication mechanism
Combined, these two settings give durable, non-duplicated producer-to-broker delivery only
A consumer crash between processing and committing its offset causes reprocessing, a duplicate the producer side can't prevent
End-to-end exactly-once requires consumer-side idempotency or Kafka transactions spanning the full read-process-write cycle

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains idempotent producers' retry-deduplication mechanism
Correctly explains acks=all as a durability, not dedup, guarantee
Correctly identifies the consumer-side gap and why it exists
Names a valid fix (idempotent consumer writes or Kafka transactions)

questions.title: Schema Registry Compatibility Modes: Backward, Forward, and Full
questions.prompt: Your team is evolving an Avro schema for an order-events topic. Explain the difference between BACKWARD, FORWARD, and FULL compatibility modes in a Schema Registry, and which one you'd pick if producers are deployed before consumers vs. the reverse.
questions.modelAnswer: BACKWARD compatibility means a new schema can read data written with the previous schema -- safe when consumers upgrade to the new schema before all old data has been consumed, since adding an optional field with a default (and old records simply missing that field) still parses fine under the new schema. FORWARD compatibility means the previous schema can read data written with the new schema -- safe when producers deploy a new schema version before consumers have upgraded, so consumers still running the old schema need to tolerate messages produced under the new one (for example, removing a field no consumer actually depended on). FULL compatibility requires both directions to hold simultaneously, which is the safest option when deploy order between producers and consumers can't be controlled or guaranteed, but it's also the most restrictive about what schema changes are even allowed. The practical decision: if producers in your organization typically deploy ahead of consumers, FORWARD is the right mode, because it's specifically checking that older consumers survive newer producer output; if consumers are deployed first to get ready for an upcoming producer change, BACKWARD is right, because it's checking that the new consumer code can still read whatever old data remains; if you can't guarantee either ordering, FULL (or FULL_TRANSITIVE, which checks against the entire schema history rather than just the immediately prior version) is the safer default.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always ask 'who deploys first here, producers or consumers' before picking a compatibility mode, because the mode name maps directly onto that deploy order. If producers typically ship first, I want FORWARD -- it's literally testing 'can an old consumer still read this new producer's output.' If consumers get upgraded ahead of time to prepare for a producer change, BACKWARD is testing the thing that actually matters: 'can this new consumer code still read the old data that's still sitting in the topic.' When I genuinely can't control or predict which side deploys first -- which is common across team boundaries -- I default to FULL, even though it's more restrictive about allowed changes, because the cost of a surprise incompatibility in production is much higher than the inconvenience of a stricter schema evolution policy.
commonMistakes: Picking BACKWARD compatibility when producers actually deploy ahead of consumers (FORWARD is the correct mode there)
Assuming any compatibility mode prevents all breaking changes, rather than just checking one specific direction
Forgetting the _TRANSITIVE variants check against the entire schema version history, not just the immediately previous version
Removing a required field without a default and expecting BACKWARD compatibility to still pass
keyPoints: BACKWARD: new schema can read data written with the old schema
FORWARD: old schema can read data written with the new schema
FULL requires both directions, at the cost of being the most restrictive on allowed changes
The right mode depends on actual producer-vs-consumer deploy order in your organization
TRANSITIVE variants check compatibility against the full schema history, not just the immediately prior version

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains BACKWARD compatibility direction
Correctly explains FORWARD compatibility direction
Correctly explains FULL and when it's the safer default
Correctly maps deploy order to the right mode choice

questions.title: Why Remote State Matters (and What Breaks Without It)
questions.prompt: A teammate on your data platform team is running terraform apply from their laptop with local state files. Explain the risks of local state for a team, what terraform remote state actually solves, and what specifically goes wrong if the state file is lost.
questions.modelAnswer: Local state means Terraform's record of what it believes exists in the cloud -- the terraform.tfstate file -- lives only on one machine, isn't shared with teammates, and isn't locked against concurrent use; if two people run apply around the same time from their own local state copies, they're each working from a view of reality that can diverge, risking corrupted state or resources created and destroyed inconsistently with what the other person's config expects. Remote state (an S3 bucket with a DynamoDB lock table, Azure Storage with blob leasing, or a managed backend like Terraform Cloud) centralizes the state file so the whole team reads and writes the same source of truth, and state locking specifically prevents two applies from running concurrently against that shared state at all. If the state file is lost entirely, Terraform no longer has any record of which real cloud resources correspond to which resources in your .tf configuration -- running apply again would attempt to create everything from scratch, which can either fail outright on resources whose names already exist, or worse, silently succeed and create duplicate infrastructure alongside now-orphaned resources that Terraform can no longer track, modify, or safely destroy. Recovering from that requires terraform import for every orphaned resource, one at a time, which is slow, manual, and genuinely error-prone at any real scale.
questions.professionalAnswer: The risk with local state isn't really about any one apply going wrong -- it's that nothing is coordinating multiple people's applies at all. Two people on a laptop-local-state team can genuinely stomp on each other's changes without either one getting an error telling them so. Remote state with locking fixes the coordination problem directly: everyone reads and writes one shared state, and the lock means only one apply can actually be in flight at a time. Losing that state file is the scenario I take most seriously, because it doesn't delete anything in the cloud -- the resources are still there, running, costing money -- it just makes Terraform blind to them. Recovering means importing every single resource back into state by hand, and on anything beyond a handful of resources that becomes a genuinely painful, slow process, which is exactly why remote state with versioning/backup on the state bucket itself is worth taking seriously from day one.
commonMistakes: Running apply from multiple laptops against separate local state copies
Not enabling state locking, allowing concurrent applies to corrupt or diverge state
Treating state loss as 'just re-run apply,' not realizing it orphans existing real resources instead of recreating them cleanly
Storing state in a plain git-tracked file, which also risks leaking any secrets present in state values
keyPoints: Local state isn't shared or locked, creating team-wide race conditions on concurrent applies
Remote state centralizes the source of truth so the whole team reads/writes the same state
State locking (e.g., a DynamoDB lock table) prevents concurrent applies from corrupting state
Losing the state file doesn't delete cloud resources, it orphans them from Terraform's tracking
Recovery after state loss requires importing every orphaned resource back into state individually

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the risk of unsynchronized local state across a team
Correctly explains what remote state plus locking actually solves
Correctly explains that state loss orphans, rather than deletes, real resources
Describes the import-based recovery path

questions.title: SCD Type 2: Why Surrogate Keys Exist and How They Work
questions.prompt: Explain why a Slowly Changing Dimension Type 2 table needs a surrogate key separate from the natural/business key, and walk through what happens to the rows when a customer's address changes.
questions.modelAnswer: In SCD Type 2, the natural key (the source system's customer_id, for example) stays identical across every historical version of that entity, but the dimension table needs to represent multiple versions of the same customer over time as separate rows, each covering a specific effective date range. If fact tables joined to the dimension using the natural key alone, there would be no way to distinguish 'customer 42 as of January' from 'customer 42 as of June' -- every fact row for that customer would join to every version of that customer indiscriminately. A surrogate key (a meaningless, auto-incrementing or hash-generated integer, unique to each version-row) solves this: fact tables store the surrogate key as their foreign key, pinning each fact to the exact dimension version that was true at the time the fact occurred, which the natural key alone could never express. When a customer's address changes: the row currently marked as current is closed out -- its valid_to is set to the change date (or an is_current flag flips to false) -- and a brand-new row is inserted with a freshly generated surrogate key, the updated address, a valid_from equal to the change date, and valid_to set to a far-future sentinel with is_current true. The natural key (customer_id) is identical on both the old and new row; only the surrogate key, the address, and the date range differ.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I'd explain the surrogate key's purpose is through the join, not the storage: a fact table has to know exactly which version of a dimension record was true when that fact happened, and the only way to express that precisely is a key that's unique per version, not per entity. The natural key -- customer_id -- is what ties all those versions back together as 'the same real customer,' but it's deliberately not what fact tables join on. When an address changes, I think of it as two separate writes: close the existing current row by setting its valid_to and flipping is_current off, then insert a new row with its own fresh surrogate key, the new address, and is_current back on. The natural key never changes across that; everything else about identifying 'the current truth' does.
commonMistakes: Using the natural key as the dimension table's primary/join key, making point-in-time history impossible to represent correctly
Forgetting to close out the old row's valid_to before inserting the new version, leaving two concurrently 'current' rows
Joining fact tables to dimensions by natural key instead of surrogate key, losing historical accuracy at query time
Not indexing on (natural_key, is_current) for fast lookup of just the current row per entity
keyPoints: The natural key identifies the real-world entity and stays constant across all its historical versions
The surrogate key identifies one specific version of that entity at a point in time
Fact tables join on the surrogate key specifically so each fact pins to the correct historical version
A change closes out the old row's valid_to/is_current and inserts a new row with a fresh surrogate key
A far-future sentinel valid_to date is the standard way to represent 'still the current row'

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why the natural key alone can't support point-in-time history
Correctly explains the surrogate key's role as a version identifier
Correctly walks through the close-out-and-insert mechanics of a change
Correctly states that the natural key is unchanged across versions

questions.title: Star Schema vs. Snowflake Schema, and Why Fact Table Grain Matters
questions.prompt: Explain the structural difference between a star schema and a snowflake schema, and why defining a fact table's grain precisely, before building anything, is one of the most consequential decisions in dimensional modeling.
questions.modelAnswer: A star schema has a central fact table surrounded directly by denormalized dimension tables, where each dimension is a single flat table even if that means repeating data -- a product dimension carrying both category and subcategory as plain columns on every row, rather than normalizing those out into their own linked tables. A snowflake schema normalizes dimensions further into related hierarchies of sub-tables (product links to subcategory, subcategory links to category, as three separate tables), trading storage redundancy for normalized structure at the cost of extra joins on every query that needs those attributes. Analytical warehouses generally favor star schemas because query engines and BI tools handle a small number of wide joins against flat dimensions better than many cascading joins through a normalized hierarchy, and the storage redundancy is cheap on modern columnar storage anyway. Fact table grain -- the precise answer to 'what does exactly one row in this table represent' -- is the single most consequential decision in the whole model because every measure, every join, and every aggregation downstream assumes a specific grain; getting it wrong, such as mixing order-level and order-line-level rows in the same fact table, or building at line-item grain but letting a report naively sum totals as if it were order-level, causes double-counting or undercounting that often stays invisible until a specific number fails to reconcile against a source system.
questions.professionalAnswer: I treat grain as the first question I answer, out loud, before writing a single CREATE TABLE statement, because every other design decision -- which dimensions to include, what the measures mean, how facts roll up -- flows from it. Star vs. snowflake is a secondary decision by comparison: I default to star for anything analytical, because the join simplicity pays for itself even with some redundant storage, and I'd only reach for snowflaking a dimension if there's a specific reason, like a genuinely huge, frequently-changing hierarchy where normalization meaningfully saves space or update cost. Where I've actually seen real damage done is grain confusion -- someone builds a fact table they believe is order-level, but a join upstream silently produces one row per order line, and every downstream SUM() is now inflated by however many lines the average order has, with nothing erroring to flag it.
commonMistakes: Mixing two different grains within a single fact table (some rows at order level, some at line-item level)
Not documenting grain explicitly, so downstream analysts guess wrong and double-count or under-count
Over-normalizing into a snowflake schema for an analytical warehouse where query simplicity matters more than storage savings
Changing a fact table's grain mid-project without migrating or notifying existing downstream consumers
keyPoints: A star schema uses flat, denormalized dimension tables joined directly to the fact table
A snowflake schema normalizes dimensions into linked hierarchies, trading storage for extra joins
Star schemas are generally preferred for analytical query performance and simplicity
Fact table grain defines what exactly one row represents, and every downstream measure depends on it
Grain mistakes (mixed grains, grain mismatches in joins) cause invisible double- or under-counting

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the structural difference between star and snowflake schemas
Correctly explains why star schemas are generally preferred analytically
Correctly explains what fact table grain means
Gives a concrete example of a grain mistake and its consequence

questions.title: The Real Cost of Lambda Architecture: Two Codepaths, Not Two Speeds
questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks why you can't 'just run the batch pipeline faster' instead of building a separate streaming path. Explain what Lambda architecture actually is, and be honest about its biggest real-world cost.
questions.modelAnswer: Lambda architecture runs two parallel processing paths over the same incoming data: a batch layer that periodically (re)computes complete, accurate views over all historical data, and a speed (streaming) layer that processes new data in near real-time to serve low-latency views before the batch layer has caught up, with a serving layer that reconciles or stitches the two outputs together for consumers. The appeal is real -- you get both correctness, because batch reprocessing can fix late-arriving data, bugs, and schema changes across the full history, and low latency, because the streaming path gives near-instant visibility into very recent events. The real, often underestimated cost is maintaining two entirely separate codebases that are supposed to implement the same business logic -- one written for a batch framework, one for a streaming framework -- and keeping them behaviorally identical as requirements evolve. In practice these two implementations drift apart: a bug fix or a new metric calculation gets implemented in one path and forgotten in the other, producing numbers that silently disagree between the real-time dashboard and the end-of-day batch report, and debugging that disagreement means tracing logic across two completely different systems written in different paradigms. This is exactly why many teams now prefer a Kappa-style approach -- one streaming engine handling both real-time processing and full reprocessing via replay -- or unified engines like Structured Streaming on Delta Lake, where one codebase and one table abstraction serve both batch and streaming needs, specifically to avoid Lambda's dual-maintenance burden.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd answer the 'just run batch faster' question honestly: speeding up batch doesn't eliminate the latency gap entirely, and it doesn't address why Lambda architecture exists in the first place for workloads that genuinely need both near-instant visibility and periodic, fully-accurate recomputation. But I wouldn't sell Lambda architecture as a free way to get both -- the cost that actually bites teams in production is maintaining the same business logic twice, once in each framework, and watching them drift apart over time as people fix bugs or add metrics in one path and forget the other. I've found that unless there's a very specific reason the two layers genuinely need different engines, a unified streaming engine that can also do full reprocessing via replay (the Kappa approach) avoids that drift entirely, because there's only one codebase computing the metric, regardless of whether it's running on live or historical data.
commonMistakes: Presenting Lambda architecture as purely a latency optimization without naming the dual-maintenance cost
Assuming the batch and streaming layers naturally stay logically consistent without active, ongoing effort
Not knowing Kappa architecture or unified batch/streaming engines exist as lower-maintenance alternatives
Underestimating how hard it is to reconcile the serving layer when the batch and streaming outputs genuinely disagree
keyPoints: Lambda architecture pairs a correctness-focused batch layer with a low-latency speed/streaming layer
A serving layer reconciles or stitches the two layers' outputs together for consumers
The real cost is maintaining duplicate business logic across two different codebases/frameworks
Drift between the two implementations causes silent, hard-to-debug numeric disagreements downstream
Kappa architecture and unified engines (Structured Streaming, Delta Lake) avoid dual maintenance by using one codebase for both

Correctly names the dual-maintenance/drift cost as the real tradeoff
Gives a concrete example of how drift manifests as disagreeing numbers
Names a valid modern alternative (Kappa or a unified engine)

deepDive.heading: Where drift actually shows up
deepDive.content: Drift rarely announces itself as an error -- it shows up as a finance analyst noticing the real-time dashboard's daily total doesn't match the batch report's total for the same day, weeks after a metric definition quietly changed in only one of the two codebases. Tracing it requires pulling up both implementations side by side and finding the one line where they diverged, which is slow precisely because the two systems don't share any code or even necessarily the same language.

deepDive.heading: Kappa as the alternative
deepDive.content: Kappa architecture treats the stream as the single source of truth and handles reprocessing by replaying the stream from an earlier offset through the same streaming job, rather than maintaining a separate batch job. This only works well when the underlying log can retain enough history to replay from, and when the streaming engine's reprocessing throughput is good enough to catch up in reasonable time -- tradeoffs worth naming explicitly rather than presenting Kappa as a strictly free upgrade over Lambda.

questions.title: Unity Catalog: Managed vs. External Table DROP Semantics
questions.prompt: An engineer runs DROP TABLE on what they thought was just a metadata pointer, and the underlying Delta files disappear from storage. Explain the difference between a managed table and an external table in Unity Catalog, and why that DROP behaved the way it did.
questions.modelAnswer: A managed table in Unity Catalog has its data files stored in a location Unity Catalog itself owns and controls, under the catalog or schema's managed storage location -- Unity Catalog treats that table's entire lifecycle, files included, as its own responsibility. An external table instead points at a location you specify explicitly, an existing path in cloud storage that already exists independently of Unity Catalog, and Unity Catalog only manages the metadata and registration for it, never the files themselves. The practical consequence is exactly what the engineer hit: DROP TABLE on a managed table deletes both the catalog entry and the actual underlying data files, because Unity Catalog owns that storage location outright and cleaning it up on drop is expected behavior. DROP TABLE on an external table removes only the catalog registration -- the underlying files are left completely untouched in their original location, since Unity Catalog never owned them to begin with. The engineer's surprise means the table in question was managed, not external; if the files needed to survive the drop, it should have been registered as external from the start, or the data should have been copied elsewhere before the drop ran.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always check DESCRIBE TABLE EXTENDED (or SHOW TABLE EXTENDED) before dropping anything I'm not completely sure about, because that's exactly where it tells you whether a table is MANAGED or EXTERNAL, and that one word changes whether DROP TABLE is a metadata-only operation or a real data deletion. Managed tables are the default in a lot of workflows, and that's fine for tables whose whole lifecycle genuinely belongs to the catalog -- but the moment data needs to be shared across catalogs, or needs to outlive a specific schema's lifecycle, or is something other teams depend on independently, I register it as external deliberately, precisely so a DROP TABLE somewhere down the line can't take the actual files out from under anyone.
commonMistakes: Assuming DROP TABLE is always a metadata-only operation regardless of table type
Not checking whether a table is managed or external before dropping it
Creating managed tables by default for data that should be shared or outlive a specific catalog/schema's lifecycle
Relying on DROP as a 'soft,' reversible operation without verifying table type first
keyPoints: Managed tables have their storage location owned by Unity Catalog, which treats the whole table lifecycle as its own
External tables point at a storage location Unity Catalog doesn't own, managing only metadata
DROP TABLE on a managed table deletes both the catalog entry and the underlying data files
DROP TABLE on an external table removes only the catalog registration, leaving files untouched
DESCRIBE/SHOW TABLE EXTENDED reveals a table's type before you drop it

Correctly explains external table storage ownership and DROP behavior
States the practical check (DESCRIBE/SHOW TABLE EXTENDED) before dropping
Gives a correct recommendation for when to use external tables deliberately

questions.title: Delta Lake's Transaction Log and Optimistic Concurrency Conflicts
questions.prompt: Two jobs write to the same Delta table at nearly the same time. Explain how the _delta_log enables ACID transactions, and what happens when both writers' changes actually conflict.
questions.modelAnswer: Every write to a Delta table is recorded as a new, sequentially numbered JSON commit file in _delta_log, listing exactly which data files were added and, for updates/deletes/merges, which files were logically removed from the table's current view; any reader or writer reconstructs the table's current state by replaying these commits in order, and that ordered, append-only commit log is what gives Delta its ACID guarantees without needing a traditional transactional database engine underneath the files. When two writers begin concurrently, each reads the table at whatever commit version was latest when it started, computes its intended changes, and attempts to commit the next sequential version number. Delta uses optimistic concurrency control: it assumes conflicts between concurrent writers are the exception rather than the rule, so it lets both proceed independently and only checks for a genuine conflict at commit time, specifically whether the files the second writer's transaction depends on were already changed by the first writer's now-committed transaction. If there's no real overlap -- both writers touched entirely different files or partitions -- the second commit succeeds by effectively rebasing onto the newly committed version. If there is a genuine overlap -- two concurrent MERGE operations both touching rows in the same underlying files -- the second writer's commit attempt fails with a concurrent-modification exception, and that transaction must retry its entire operation against the table's latest state rather than silently corrupting anything.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe _delta_log as the actual mechanism, not just an audit trail -- every commit is a small JSON file describing exactly what changed, and the table's current state is just the result of replaying all of them in order. That's what lets two jobs write at the same time safely: Delta doesn't lock the whole table for every write, it optimistically lets both attempts proceed and only arbitrates at the moment of commit, checking whether the specific files involved actually overlap. Most of the time, especially with well-partitioned data, two concurrent writers touch different files entirely and both commits sail through with no conflict at all. When they do genuinely overlap, Delta fails the second writer's commit outright rather than quietly merging something incorrectly, and the calling code needs to be written to catch that specific exception and retry the whole operation against the now-current table state -- that's expected, normal behavior for a system under real concurrent write load, not a bug to suppress.
commonMistakes: Assuming Delta serializes every concurrent write rather than optimistically allowing non-conflicting ones in parallel
Not catching and retrying concurrent-modification exceptions in pipeline code, treating them as unexpected failures
Writing to the same partition from multiple uncoordinated jobs with no retry strategy at all
Believing _delta_log is just an audit log rather than the actual mechanism providing atomicity and consistency
keyPoints: _delta_log is an ordered sequence of JSON commits describing added and removed files
A reader or writer derives the table's current state by replaying those commits in order
Delta uses optimistic concurrency control, letting non-conflicting concurrent writes both succeed
A genuine conflict (overlapping files) fails the second writer's commit with a concurrent-modification exception
Pipeline code should expect and retry concurrent-modification exceptions as normal behavior under concurrent writes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the transaction log's structure and role in ACID guarantees
Correctly explains optimistic concurrency's assume-no-conflict approach
Correctly explains what happens on a genuine file-level conflict
Mentions retry as the correct handling for a concurrent-modification failure

questions.title: Snowflake Time Travel vs. Fail-safe: Who Can Recover What, and When
questions.prompt: A table was accidentally truncated three days ago, and the retention period is the standard default. Explain the difference between Snowflake's Time Travel and Fail-safe, and whether this data is still recoverable, and by whom.
questions.modelAnswer: Time Travel lets you query, clone, or restore a table's historical state within its configured retention window -- 1 day by default on Standard edition, configurable up to 90 days on Enterprise and above for permanent tables -- using AT/BEFORE clauses or UNDROP, and critically, any user with appropriate privileges on the table or schema can self-serve this recovery with no support ticket required. Fail-safe is a separate, fixed, non-configurable 7-day period that begins the moment Time Travel's retention window ends; during Fail-safe, data is recoverable only by contacting Snowflake Support directly, since it exists purely as a disaster-recovery backstop with no self-service SQL interface at all. For a table truncated three days ago: on Standard edition with the default 1-day Time Travel retention, that data has already passed out of Time Travel and into Fail-safe, meaning recovery requires a Snowflake Support request rather than any SQL the user can run themselves; on Enterprise or higher with retention set to 7 or more days, the data is still within Time Travel and fully self-service recoverable via UNDROP TABLE (for a drop) or a point-in-time SELECT ... AT(timestamp => ...) combined with an INSERT (for a truncate, since UNDROP doesn't apply to a TRUNCATE).
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd check is DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS on the specific table, because that number is what decides whether this is a five-minute self-service fix or a support ticket. If Time Travel retention covers three days, I'd just query the table as of just before the truncate with the AT clause and re-insert the data myself. If it doesn't -- which is the Standard edition default -- the data has already moved into Fail-safe, and there's no SQL I can run to get it back; it becomes a conversation with Snowflake Support, and I'd set the expectation with whoever's asking that this isn't instant and isn't guaranteed to be fast, since Fail-safe is explicitly a backstop for genuine disaster recovery, not a user-facing undo button.
commonMistakes: Assuming Fail-safe is self-service the same way Time Travel is
Not knowing the default Time Travel retention differs by edition, capping at 1 day on Standard
Confusing Time Travel's AT/BEFORE query capability with a full backup/restore system
Not checking the specific table's DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS before assuming the data is unrecoverable
keyPoints: Time Travel is self-service and configurable (0-90 days depending on edition), queryable via AT/BEFORE and UNDROP
Fail-safe is a fixed 7-day window after Time Travel expires, recoverable only through Snowflake Support
Whether recovery is self-service depends entirely on how long ago the event happened versus the table's configured retention
Edition determines the maximum configurable Time Travel retention period
UNDROP works for a dropped object, while a truncate requires a point-in-time query plus a manual re-insert

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains Time Travel's self-service, configurable nature
Correctly explains Fail-safe's fixed, Support-only nature
Correctly determines recoverability based on retention vs. elapsed time
Distinguishes the recovery mechanism for a drop (UNDROP) vs. a truncate (AT + re-insert)

questions.title: Writing a dbt Incremental Model with the Merge Strategy
questions.prompt: Write a dbt SQL model for fct_orders that is materialized as incremental using the merge strategy, keyed on order_id, that only processes orders updated since the last run using a lookback window to handle late-arriving updates.
questions.modelAnswer: The config block sets materialized='incremental' and unique_key='order_id', which tells dbt what to match on when it performs the merge; incremental_strategy='merge' makes that upsert behavior explicit rather than relying on an adapter's default. The is_incremental() guard wraps the WHERE clause so it only applies on runs where the target table already exists -- on the first build or a --full-refresh, the whole source loads unfiltered. Instead of a strict updated_at > max(updated_at) boundary, the filter uses a three-day lookback (dateadd(day, -3, max(updated_at))) so that any update which arrives a little late relative to when it logically happened still gets picked up and re-merged, rather than being silently skipped forever by a boundary that only ever looks forward. Because the model merges on order_id, re-processing those three days of data on every run doesn't create duplicates -- rows already loaded are simply matched and updated to the same (or newly changed) values.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through why each piece of the config is there rather than just reading the code back. unique_key plus incremental_strategy='merge' together are what make this idempotent -- without both, a rerun risks either duplicating rows or silently doing a plain append. The lookback window is the detail I'd call out as the one most people get wrong on their first incremental model: a strict greater-than boundary feels correct until an order update arrives a day late, and then it's just gone, with no error anywhere telling you it happened. I'd also mention I always test this model with a full --full-refresh run at least once in CI, specifically to confirm the unfiltered first-run path (where is_incremental() is false) still produces correct results, not just the incremental path.
commonMistakes: Using incremental_strategy='append' on a source where rows get updated, causing duplicate order_id rows over time
Omitting the lookback window and silently dropping orders that update later than the current max
Forgetting unique_key, which makes a real merge impossible and risks falling back to unsafe append-like behavior
Never testing the model with --full-refresh to confirm correct behavior on the unfiltered first run
keyPoints: unique_key combined with incremental_strategy='merge' gives idempotent upserts safe to rerun
is_incremental() scopes the WHERE filter to only apply on runs where the table already exists
A lookback window (rather than a strict boundary) protects against late-arriving updates
Re-processing the lookback window doesn't create duplicates because the merge matches on order_id
The first run (or a full-refresh) must still produce correct results with is_incremental() false

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly configures materialized, unique_key, and incremental_strategy
Correctly implements the is_incremental() guard
Correctly implements a lookback window instead of a strict boundary
Explains why this configuration is safe to rerun without duplication

questions.title: Writing an Idempotent Fact-Table Upsert with MERGE
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL MERGE statement that loads daily sales facts into fct_sales from a staging table, matching on the natural key (order_id, line_number), updating changed rows, and inserting new ones, in a way that's safe to re-run if the same day's batch is reprocessed.
questions.code:
MERGE fct_sales AS target
USING stg_sales AS source
    ON target.order_id = source.order_id
   AND target.line_number = source.line_number
WHEN MATCHED AND (
        target.quantity <> source.quantity
     OR target.unit_price <> source.unit_price
     OR target.updated_at <> source.updated_at
    )
THEN UPDATE SET
    target.quantity = source.quantity,
    target.unit_price = source.unit_price,
    target.updated_at = source.updated_at
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET THEN
    INSERT (order_id, line_number, quantity, unit_price, updated_at)
    VALUES (source.order_id, source.line_number, source.quantity, source.unit_price, source.updated_at);
questions.modelAnswer: The composite natural key (order_id, line_number) is what makes re-running the same batch safe: the same staging row always matches the same target row, rather than ever inserting a duplicate line. The WHEN MATCHED clause includes an explicit change-detection condition rather than unconditionally updating every matched row -- without it, every single row gets rewritten on every run even when nothing actually changed, which is wasted write volume at any real scale. WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET handles genuinely new lines. Deliberately absent here is a WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE DELETE clause, because this is an additive daily batch load, not a full-state sync -- adding that clause would delete every historical fact row not present in today's staging batch, which would be catastrophic; it would only belong in a MERGE where staging represents the complete, current universe of all facts, not just one day's increment.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out the change-detection condition inside WHEN MATCHED as the detail that separates a correct MERGE from a technically-working-but-wasteful one -- without it, you're rewriting every single row on every single run regardless of whether anything changed, which shows up as unnecessary I/O and log growth at scale. I'd also flag the missing WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE clause as intentional, not an oversight -- adding a DELETE there on a batch load that only represents one day's data would wipe out every other day's historical facts, since 'not matched by source' would be true for all of them. That clause only makes sense when the source genuinely represents the full current state of everything.
commonMistakes: Matching on a non-unique or incomplete key (e.g., order_id alone) when the real fact grain is per line
Omitting the change-detection condition in WHEN MATCHED, causing every row to be rewritten every run even when unchanged
Adding WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE DELETE on a batch load instead of a full sync, accidentally deleting valid historical rows
Not wrapping the MERGE in a transaction when multiple related tables need to update together atomically
keyPoints: Match on the full natural/composite key that actually defines the fact table's grain
A change-detection condition in WHEN MATCHED avoids unnecessary rewrites of unchanged rows
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET handles new rows idempotently on reruns
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE DELETE is only correct for full-state syncs, never for incremental batch loads
Re-running the same batch is safe because the natural key ensures matching rows update rather than duplicate

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly matches on the composite natural key defining fact grain
Correctly includes a change-detection condition to avoid unnecessary updates
Correctly handles new rows via WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET
Correctly explains why WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE DELETE would be wrong here

questions.title: Writing an Airflow TaskFlow DAG with Automatic XCom Wiring
questions.prompt: Write a small Airflow DAG using the TaskFlow API (@dag/@task decorators) that extracts a list of records, transforms them, and loads them, passing data between tasks without manually calling xcom_push/xcom_pull.
questions.modelAnswer: The @task decorator turns a plain Python function into an Airflow task, and calling one task's return value as the argument to another -- load(transform(extract())) -- automatically wires an XCom push and pull behind the scenes, with no explicit ti.xcom_push/ti.xcom_pull calls and no manual task_id string references needed; Airflow infers both the data flow and the task dependency graph directly from that function call structure. This pattern fits small-to-medium payloads well, since XCom values are stored in the metadata database (or a configured external XCom backend) -- passing multi-gigabyte datasets this way would bloat that storage and slow the scheduler, so large data should be passed by reference instead (a file path, a table name, a URI) rather than through the TaskFlow return value directly. catchup=False means that deploying this DAG won't trigger it to run for every historical interval since start_date, only going forward from now.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point at the single line load(transform(extract())) as the whole story here -- that's not just calling three functions, it's Airflow building both the task dependency graph and the XCom wiring purely from how I called them. I don't write a single xcom_push or xcom_pull anywhere. The thing I'd watch for in review is payload size: TaskFlow makes it so easy to pass data between tasks that people start passing entire dataframes through return values, and that's exactly the kind of thing that bloats the metadata database and slows the whole scheduler down. My rule of thumb is if it fits comfortably as a small list of dicts or a scalar, TaskFlow return values are great; if it's a real dataset, I pass a reference instead and let the next task load it itself.
commonMistakes: Passing large datasets directly through XCom/TaskFlow return values instead of passing a reference
Forgetting catchup=False when backfilling every missed interval since start_date isn't desired on deploy
Mixing TaskFlow tasks with classic operators without understanding how XComArg wiring interacts with explicit dependency declarations
Not type-hinting task functions, making the DAG's data flow harder to reason about at a glance
keyPoints: TaskFlow's @task decorator turns a function into a task with inferred dependencies from the call graph
Calling one task's output as another's input auto-wires XCom with no manual push/pull calls
XCom values live in the metadata database (or an external backend), so large payloads should be passed by reference instead
catchup controls whether every missed historical interval runs automatically on deploy
Task dependencies and data flow are both derived from the same function-call structure in TaskFlow

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses @dag/@task decorators with inferred dependencies
Correctly explains the automatic XCom wiring mechanism
Correctly identifies the payload-size limitation and the pass-by-reference alternative
Provides a valid, runnable DAG structure

questions.title: Branching Logic Combined with Trigger Rules in Airflow
questions.prompt: Write an Airflow DAG where a BranchPythonOperator decides between a 'full load' path and an 'incremental load' path, and a downstream notify_success task should run if either branch succeeds, even though the other branch was skipped. Show the trigger_rule that makes this work.
questions.code:
from airflow.operators.python import BranchPythonOperator, PythonOperator
from airflow.utils.trigger_rule import TriggerRule
from airflow import DAG
from datetime import datetime

def choose_branch(**context):
    return "full_load" if context["ds"].endswith("01") else "incremental_load"

with DAG("load_dag", schedule="@daily", start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1), catchup=False) as dag:
    branch = BranchPythonOperator(task_id="choose_branch", python_callable=choose_branch)
    full_load = PythonOperator(task_id="full_load", python_callable=lambda: print("full"))
    incremental_load = PythonOperator(task_id="incremental_load", python_callable=lambda: print("incremental"))
    notify_success = PythonOperator(
        task_id="notify_success",
        python_callable=lambda: print("notifying"),
        trigger_rule=TriggerRule.NONE_FAILED_MIN_ONE_SUCCESS,
    )

    branch >> [full_load, incremental_load] >> notify_success
questions.modelAnswer: The default trigger_rule, all_success, would never actually fire notify_success here, because exactly one of the two upstream branches is always marked skipped (not failed) by BranchPythonOperator's design, and all_success treats a skipped upstream task as not satisfying the rule -- the downstream task would itself end up skipped forever, propagating the skip rather than running. none_failed_min_one_success is the correct rule for this exact join pattern: it fires as long as nothing upstream genuinely failed and at least one upstream task actually succeeded, which correctly tolerates the unchosen branch's skip while still requiring real confirmation that the chosen branch ran successfully. The alternative none_failed (without the min-one-success requirement) would also tolerate the skip, but would fire even if every upstream task were skipped, which isn't what's wanted here -- you want proof something actually ran, not merely that nothing failed.
questions.professionalAnswer: The trigger_rule line is the whole answer to this question -- everything else is standard branching setup. I'd explain why I didn't just leave the default: all_success looks fine until you realize one branch is deliberately skipped every single run by design, and all_success propagates that skip right through to notify_success, so it would never fire. none_failed_min_one_success is specifically built for a branch-then-join pattern like this: tolerate the expected skip, but still require real evidence that the branch that did run actually succeeded, rather than just 'nothing exploded.'
commonMistakes: Leaving the join task at the default all_success trigger rule and watching it get skipped forever
Using none_failed instead of none_failed_min_one_success, which would also fire if every branch happened to be skipped
Forgetting BranchPythonOperator's callable must return the exact downstream task_id string(s), not an arbitrary value
Not accounting for how skip status propagates differently depending on the chosen trigger rule for tasks further downstream
keyPoints: Default all_success trigger rule fails at a branch join because the unchosen branch is always skipped
none_failed_min_one_success tolerates expected skips while still requiring at least one real success
none_failed alone would also fire even if every branch were skipped, which isn't the intent here
BranchPythonOperator's return value must match actual downstream task_id(s) exactly
Trigger rules determine how skip/failure status propagates at any join point in a DAG

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies why the default trigger rule fails at this join
Correctly selects none_failed_min_one_success and explains why over alternatives
Provides a valid, correctly structured branching DAG
Correctly implements the branch callable returning valid task_id(s)

questions.title: Diagnosing Partition Assignment After a Consumer Joins a Group
questions.prompt: A topic has 12 partitions and a consumer group currently has 4 consumer instances, each handling 3 partitions. The team adds 8 more consumer instances to the same group to scale up, bringing the group to 12 consumers total. Walk through exactly what happens during the rebalance, and what the behavior would be if the team had instead added enough consumers to exceed the partition count.
questions.modelAnswer: When a new consumer joins an existing group, the group coordinator triggers a rebalance -- every consumer in the group briefly pauses processing while the coordinator, using the configured partition assignment strategy (range, round-robin, or the cooperative sticky assignor), redistributes all 12 partitions across the now-12 consumer instances. With exactly 12 partitions and 12 consumers, the ideal and actual outcome is one partition per consumer, giving maximum parallelism for this topic. If the team had instead added enough consumers to exceed the partition count -- say 16 total consumers for 12 partitions -- Kafka cannot assign more than one active consumer to the same partition within a single consumer group, since that per-partition exclusivity is exactly the mechanism that gives ordered, non-overlapping processing within a group; any consumer instance beyond the partition count would receive zero partitions and sit completely idle, consuming nothing, functioning only as a hot standby that would pick up a partition automatically if an active consumer dropped out and triggered another rebalance.
questions.professionalAnswer: The practical ceiling I always explain to people scaling a consumer group is partition count, full stop -- adding the 9th through 12th consumer in this scenario genuinely helps, since there are exactly enough partitions to go around, but anything past that point stops helping no matter how many more instances get added, because Kafka will simply never assign a 13th consumer an active partition in that group. I'd also flag the rebalance mechanics themselves as worth knowing: with the older eager assignors (range, round-robin), the whole group stops processing during the rebalance while every partition gets reassigned, even ones that didn't need to move; the cooperative sticky assignor reduces that disruption by only reassigning the specific partitions that actually need to move.
commonMistakes: Assuming adding more consumers always linearly increases throughput regardless of partition count
Not realizing idle consumers beyond the partition count are expected behavior, not a misconfiguration
Using the eager range/round-robin assignor without realizing it causes a full group-wide pause during rebalance
Forgetting partition count is the hard ceiling on active parallelism, so scaling consumers past it requires increasing partitions instead
keyPoints: Partition count is the hard ceiling on active, concurrent consumer parallelism within one consumer group
A rebalance redistributes partitions across the group whenever membership changes
With consumers equal to partitions, the ideal outcome is exactly one partition per consumer
Consumers beyond the partition count sit completely idle as standby, consuming nothing
The cooperative sticky assignor reduces rebalance disruption compared to eager assignors like range or round-robin

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what triggers and happens during a rebalance
Correctly explains the one-active-consumer-per-partition exclusivity within a group
Correctly explains the idle-standby behavior when consumers exceed partitions
Mentions the eager vs. cooperative sticky assignor distinction

questions.title: Writing a Terraform Module and Importing a Hand-Created Resource Into It
questions.prompt: Your team has a storage account that was created manually in the Azure portal before Terraform was adopted. Write the Terraform resource block and the import command needed to bring it under Terraform management without recreating it, and explain why you'd check terraform plan carefully right after.
questions.code:
resource "azurerm_storage_account" "landing" {
  name                     = "ltvlandingzone01"
  resource_group_name      = azurerm_resource_group.data.name
  location                 = "eastus"
  account_tier             = "Standard"
  account_replication_type = "LRS"
}

# terraform import azurerm_storage_account.landing \
#   /subscriptions/<sub-id>/resourceGroups/<rg-name>/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/ltvlandingzone01
questions.modelAnswer: terraform import binds an existing real-world resource, identified by its full cloud provider resource ID, to a resource address already declared in .tf configuration, without creating or destroying anything -- it only writes an entry into Terraform's state file. The .tf resource block has to already exist, and its arguments need to be written to match the real resource's actual current configuration as closely as possible, because classic import only populates state, it does not generate the matching configuration for you; any mismatch between what's written in config and what the resource actually looks like in the cloud shows up immediately on the very next plan as a diff Terraform wants to 'correct' -- and some of those corrections (like account_tier, which can force replacement on certain storage account changes) would be genuinely destructive if accepted. That's exactly why terraform plan has to be read line by line immediately after an import, before ever running apply: a clean plan with no changes confirms the written config truly matches reality, while any unexpected diff needs to be fixed in the configuration itself, never just accepted by applying it blindly.
questions.professionalAnswer: The sequence I always follow is: write the resource block first, matching the real resource's settings as exactly as I can determine them, then run the import command, then immediately run plan and read every single line before touching apply. The reason I'm strict about that last step is that import only updates state -- it doesn't write or fix my .tf file for me in the classic workflow, so any attribute I got slightly wrong in the config is sitting there as a live diff waiting to 'fix' the real resource the next time someone runs apply, and for something like account_tier that fix could mean an actual destroy-and-recreate on a resource real workloads already depend on.
commonMistakes: Assuming import also writes or corrects the resource block's arguments for you
Running apply immediately after import without reading plan output first
Importing into the wrong resource address, silently mismatching the logical and real resource
Not realizing the resource ID format is provider- and resource-type-specific and getting it wrong
keyPoints: terraform import binds an existing resource to a resource address in state, without recreating it
The .tf config must be written to match the real resource's actual settings as closely as possible
Import only updates state in the classic workflow; it does not generate matching configuration automatically
A mismatch between config and reality shows up as a diff on the very next plan, which could be destructive if applied
Always review plan line by line immediately after import, before ever running apply

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly writes a valid resource block matching the real resource

questions.title: Writing a GitHub Actions Workflow That Gates Merges on a Passing dbt build
questions.prompt: Write a GitHub Actions workflow triggered on pull requests against main that runs dbt build (not separate dbt run + dbt test) against a PR-specific schema, and explain how this becomes an actual required status check that blocks merging.
questions.code:
name: dbt-ci
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  dbt-build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"
      - run: pip install dbt-snowflake
      - name: dbt build (PR schema)
        env:
          DBT_SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT: ${{ secrets.DBT_SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT }}
          DBT_SNOWFLAKE_USER: ${{ secrets.DBT_SNOWFLAKE_USER }}
          DBT_SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.DBT_SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD }}
        run: |
          dbt deps
          dbt build --target ci --vars '{"schema_suffix": "pr_${{ github.event.number }}"}'
questions.modelAnswer: dbt build runs seed, run, snapshot, and test together in dependency order per model, rather than running the whole model DAG first and testing it entirely afterward -- this means a failing test on one model blocks that specific model's downstream dependents from building on top of already-known-bad data within the same invocation, which a separate dbt run followed by dbt test cannot do, since test only runs after every model has already finished building regardless of whether an upstream model's data was already wrong. Scoping the build to a PR-specific schema (via a vars-driven suffix tied to the PR number) isolates every pull request's build into its own schema, so concurrent PRs never collide over the same objects, and this same isolation is also the foundation that later enables dbt's Slim CI state:modified+ and deferral workflow. For this workflow to actually block a bad merge, it must be explicitly configured as a required status check in GitHub's branch protection settings (Settings > Branches > branch protection rule > Require status checks to pass), referencing this exact job by name -- without that one setting, the workflow still runs and reports a result, but a PR can be merged regardless of whether it passed or failed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd be specific that writing the YAML is only half of this -- a CI workflow that just runs and reports red or green doesn't block anything on its own. The piece people forget is going into branch protection settings and explicitly marking this job as a required status check; until that's done, main's merge button doesn't care what this workflow says. On the workflow itself, I always reach for dbt build over separate run and test commands specifically because of the ordering guarantee -- I don't want a model two layers downstream of a failing test to build on top of data that's already known to be wrong, and build's per-model interleaving is what prevents that within a single CI run.
