questions.title: Implementing SCD Type 2 with a Coordinated MERGE and Insert
questions.prompt: Write the SQL against dim_customer that correctly implements SCD Type 2 for incoming customer data in stg_customer, closing out the old row's valid_to and inserting a new current row whenever tracked attributes (like address or segment) change.
questions.code:
MERGE dim_customer AS target
USING stg_customer AS source
    ON target.customer_id = source.customer_id
   AND target.is_current = 1
WHEN MATCHED AND (
        target.address <> source.address
     OR target.segment <> source.segment
    )
THEN UPDATE SET
    target.is_current = 0,
    target.valid_to = CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE)
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET THEN
    INSERT (customer_id, address, segment, valid_from, valid_to, is_current)
    VALUES (source.customer_id, source.address, source.segment, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE), '9999-12-31', 1);

-- Second pass: insert the new current row for every customer just closed out above
INSERT INTO dim_customer (customer_id, address, segment, valid_from, valid_to, is_current)
SELECT s.customer_id, s.address, s.segment, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE), '9999-12-31', 1
FROM stg_customer s
JOIN dim_customer d
  ON d.customer_id = s.customer_id AND d.is_current = 0 AND d.valid_to = CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE)
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM dim_customer d2 WHERE d2.customer_id = s.customer_id AND d2.is_current = 1
);
questions.modelAnswer: A single MERGE statement can't both close an old row and insert a brand-new version row for the same logical key in standard T-SQL, because MERGE can only apply one action -- update or insert -- per matched source row, not both for the same key in one pass. Real SCD2 implementations in T-SQL therefore typically use two coordinated statements: the MERGE detects changed or brand-new customers and either closes out the existing current row (is_current = 0, valid_to = today) when something tracked actually changed, or inserts a first-ever row for a customer that's never been seen before; a second INSERT statement then adds the fresh current-version row for every customer that was just closed out in the first step, identified by joining stg_customer back to the rows that now have is_current = 0 and a valid_to of today, but no existing is_current = 1 row yet. The WHEN MATCHED join condition filters specifically to is_current = 1 so the comparison is always against the live row, never an older historical version.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd be upfront that this is one of the few patterns where a single statement genuinely can't do the whole job in T-SQL -- MERGE updates or inserts per matched row, it can't do both for the same key in one pass, so closing an old version and opening a new one has to be two coordinated steps. I'd also mention that engines and tools with richer MERGE semantics, or dbt's built-in snapshot feature, automate this exact two-step pattern for you, generating the valid_from/valid_to columns automatically -- which is usually what I'd actually reach for in a real pipeline rather than hand-rolling this twice every time a new SCD2 dimension comes up.
commonMistakes: Trying to force the entire close-and-insert logic into one MERGE statement when the engine doesn't support it
Joining on customer_id alone without filtering to is_current = 1, comparing against a stale historical row instead of the live one
Forgetting the far-future sentinel valid_to date for the first-time insert branch
Not indexing on (customer_id, is_current) for fast lookup of the current row
keyPoints: SCD2 often needs two coordinated statements in T-SQL, since one MERGE can't update-and-insert for the same key
The MERGE's match condition must filter to is_current = 1 to always compare against the live row
Closing out a row means setting is_current = 0 and valid_to to the change date
A second INSERT adds the fresh current row for every customer just closed out in the first step
Tools like dbt snapshots can automate this entire pattern rather than hand-writing it each time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why one MERGE can't close-and-insert for the same key
Correctly filters the match condition to the live row via is_current
Correctly implements the two-step close-then-insert logic
Mentions a real automation alternative (dbt snapshots or equivalent)

questions.title: Building an Incremental Pipeline with Snowflake Streams and Tasks
questions.prompt: Write the Snowflake SQL to create a stream on a raw orders table and a task that incrementally processes only the changed rows from that stream into a cleaned table every 5 minutes.
questions.code:
CREATE OR REPLACE STREAM orders_stream ON TABLE raw.orders;

CREATE OR REPLACE TASK process_orders_task
  WAREHOUSE = etl_wh
  SCHEDULE = '5 MINUTE'
WHEN
  SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('orders_stream')
AS
  MERGE INTO clean.orders AS target
  USING orders_stream AS source
      ON target.order_id = source.order_id
  WHEN MATCHED AND source.METADATA$ACTION = 'DELETE' THEN DELETE
  WHEN MATCHED AND source.METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT' THEN
      UPDATE SET target.status = source.status, target.updated_at = source.updated_at
  WHEN NOT MATCHED AND source.METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT' THEN
      INSERT (order_id, status, updated_at) VALUES (source.order_id, source.status, source.updated_at);

ALTER TASK process_orders_task RESUME;
questions.modelAnswer: A Stream is a change-tracking object that records every insert, update, and delete made to a table since the stream was last consumed, exposed through METADATA$ACTION, METADATA$ISUPDATE, and METADATA$ROW_ID columns, without needing a separate watermark or ingestion-timestamp column to track progress -- consuming the stream, meaning reading it inside a DML statement like the MERGE here, atomically advances its internal offset, so each change row is processed exactly once even across many separate task runs. The task's WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA(...) clause is a cost-control guard: the task still wakes up on its five-minute schedule, but it skips executing the warehouse-consuming MERGE entirely whenever the stream has nothing new, avoiding paying for compute on empty cycles. Tasks are created in a suspended state by default, so ALTER TASK ... RESUME is required before the schedule actually starts firing. An updated row typically appears in a standard stream as a paired delete-then-insert (with METADATA$ISUPDATE = TRUE on the insert half) rather than a single row, which the MERGE's WHEN MATCHED/WHEN NOT MATCHED branches handle correctly as written.
questions.professionalAnswer: The two things I'd make sure not to skip when setting this up are resuming the task -- it's silently suspended by default and will just never run otherwise -- and the WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA guard, which saves real warehouse credits by skipping the MERGE on the cycles where nothing actually changed. I'd also explain that 'consuming' a stream isn't a separate step -- simply reading from it inside this MERGE is what advances its offset, so there's no explicit 'mark as consumed' call needed, which is easy to not realize the first time you work with one.
commonMistakes: Forgetting tasks are created SUSPENDED by default and never resuming them
Querying a stream outside of a DML transaction and assuming the offset advanced anyway
Not using WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA, wasting warehouse credits on empty scheduled runs
Assuming a standard stream behaves like an append-only log rather than representing row-level changes including deletes
keyPoints: A Stream tracks row-level inserts/updates/deletes since it was last consumed, with an automatically advancing offset
Consuming a stream means reading it inside a DML statement; no separate 'mark as consumed' step exists
Tasks are suspended by default and must be explicitly resumed to start running on schedule
WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA avoids wasted compute on scheduled runs where nothing changed
An update typically appears in a stream as a paired delete-then-insert, which MERGE's branches handle correctly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly creates a stream on the source table
Correctly implements the task with a schedule and stream-has-data guard
Correctly explains how stream consumption/offset advancement works
Mentions that tasks must be resumed after creation

questions.title: Using foreachBatch to Bridge Structured Streaming into a Delta MERGE
questions.prompt: Write PySpark code for a Structured Streaming job reading from a Kafka source that needs to upsert into a Delta table using MERGE, something Structured Streaming's native sinks can't do directly. Show how foreachBatch solves this.
questions.code:
from delta.tables import DeltaTable
from pyspark.sql.functions import col, from_json

def upsert_to_delta(microbatch_df, batch_id):
    target = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "silver.customer_events")
    (target.alias("t")
        .merge(microbatch_df.alias("s"), "t.customer_id = s.customer_id")
        .whenMatchedUpdateAll()
        .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
        .execute())

stream_df = (spark.readStream
    .format("kafka")
    .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "broker:9092")
    .option("subscribe", "customer-events")
    .load())

parsed_df = (stream_df.selectExpr("CAST(value AS STRING) as json")
    .select(from_json(col("json"), event_schema).alias("data"))
    .select("data.*"))

(parsed_df.writeStream
    .foreachBatch(upsert_to_delta)
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/checkpoints/customer_events")
    .trigger(processingTime="1 minute")
    .start())
questions.modelAnswer: Structured Streaming's native streaming sinks are built around append-only output and have no built-in upsert semantics at all. foreachBatch converts the otherwise continuous streaming DataFrame into a sequence of discrete micro-batches, each delivered to your callback function as a regular, non-streaming DataFrame -- which means any batch API is available inside it, including DeltaTable.merge(), an operation that simply doesn't exist as a native streaming sink option. Each micro-batch's MERGE is itself its own atomic Delta transaction, fully consistent with everything discussed about Delta's transaction log. The checkpointLocation tracks exactly which Kafka offsets have already been processed, so if the job restarts after a failure, it resumes from precisely where it left off rather than reprocessing already-handled messages or skipping unprocessed ones -- which is what makes the overall pipeline idempotent even though MERGE is technically being invoked once per micro-batch rather than once per individual message.
questions.professionalAnswer: The key realization I'd walk through is that foreachBatch isn't really 'streaming logic' at all -- it hands you a perfectly ordinary batch DataFrame once per micro-batch, and from that point on you write completely normal batch code, including a Delta MERGE that would never be available as a direct streaming sink. The piece that's easy to get wrong is forgetting the checkpoint location is what gives this exactly-once-style guarantee on restart -- without it, a crash between the MERGE committing and Spark's own tracking catching up could mean reprocessing or skipping data on the next run.
commonMistakes: Trying to call DeltaTable.merge() directly on the streaming DataFrame without going through foreachBatch
Forgetting the checkpoint location, which breaks consistent offset tracking and recovery on restart
Not making the merge logic itself idempotent in case a batch gets reprocessed after a failure between processing and checkpoint commit
Setting the trigger interval so short that MERGE overhead per micro-batch dominates total runtime
keyPoints: Native streaming sinks support append-only output only, with no built-in upsert capability
foreachBatch delivers each micro-batch as an ordinary batch DataFrame where batch APIs like DeltaTable.merge() work
Checkpointing tracks processed Kafka offsets, enabling consistent recovery after a restart
Each micro-batch's MERGE is its own atomic Delta transaction
The merge logic itself should be idempotent, since a micro-batch could be reprocessed after certain failure scenarios

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why native streaming sinks can't perform a MERGE directly
Correctly explains foreachBatch's role in bridging to batch APIs
Correctly explains the checkpoint's role in exactly-once-style recovery
Provides valid, correctly structured PySpark code

questions.title: Writing Star Schema DDL with Surrogate Keys and a Date Dimension
questions.prompt: Write the DDL for a simple star schema: a fact_sales table at order-line grain, a dim_product table, and a dim_date table, using surrogate keys throughout rather than natural keys as the join columns.
questions.code:
CREATE TABLE dim_date (
    date_key       INT PRIMARY KEY,        -- surrogate, e.g. 20260301
    full_date      DATE NOT NULL,
    day_of_week    VARCHAR(10),
    month_name     VARCHAR(10),
    fiscal_quarter TINYINT
);

CREATE TABLE dim_product (
    product_key    INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,  -- surrogate
    product_id     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,            -- natural key from source
    product_name   VARCHAR(200),
    category       VARCHAR(100),
    is_current     BIT DEFAULT 1
);

CREATE TABLE fact_sales (
    sale_key       BIGINT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
    order_id       VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    line_number    INT NOT NULL,
    date_key       INT NOT NULL REFERENCES dim_date(date_key),
    product_key    INT NOT NULL REFERENCES dim_product(product_key),
    quantity       INT NOT NULL,
    net_amount     DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL
);
questions.modelAnswer: fact_sales joins to its dimensions only through surrogate keys (date_key, product_key), never through natural keys like product_id -- this is specifically what allows dim_product to carry SCD Type 2 history (multiple product_key versions per product_id over time) without any ambiguity about which version a given fact row actually relates to. dim_date is a pre-populated, static dimension, one row per calendar day typically spanning many years, using a smart integer surrogate key (YYYYMMDD format) that's both meaningful for sorting and partition pruning and still a dimension-controlled key rather than a raw date value derived ad hoc in every query. The fact table's grain is explicit by construction -- order_id plus line_number together identify exactly one row -- and that decision drives the meaning of every measure in the table; net_amount is a per-line value, not a per-order total, and any report needing order-level totals must explicitly re-aggregate up from this grain rather than assuming it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point to the two foreign keys on fact_sales as the actual design decision worth defending -- date_key and product_key are both surrogate, generated and owned by their dimension tables, never the raw natural identifiers from source systems. That's what lets dim_product track SCD2 history cleanly: a given product_id can have several rows over time, each with its own product_key, and a fact row joins to exactly the one that was true when the sale happened. I'd also flag dim_date specifically -- I always build a real, pre-populated date dimension rather than relying on raw DATE columns and deriving calendar attributes in every query, because it's cheap to build once and it keeps every report's definition of 'fiscal quarter' or 'day of week' consistent.

Omitting a dedicated date dimension and deriving calendar attributes ad hoc from raw DATE columns in every query
Not documenting grain explicitly, leaving future developers to assume order-level when it's actually line-level
Using a plain IDENTITY instead of a meaningful YYYYMMDD integer for the date dimension's key

dim_product's natural key (product_id) persists across SCD2 versions, each with its own surrogate product_key

Order-level totals must be explicitly re-aggregated from line-level grain, not assumed

questions.title: Writing a Silver-Layer Transform in a Medallion Pipeline
questions.prompt: Write a PySpark job that reads raw bronze-layer customer order events (JSON, as-landed, with duplicates and some malformed rows), and produces a cleaned silver-layer Delta table: deduplicated, schema-validated, and with bad rows routed to a quarantine table instead of silently dropped.
questions.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

bronze_df = spark.read.format("delta").load("/bronze/order_events")

parsed_df = bronze_df.withColumn(
    "is_valid",
    F.col("order_id").isNotNull() & F.col("amount").cast("double").isNotNull()
)

valid_df = parsed_df.filter("is_valid")
quarantine_df = parsed_df.filter("NOT is_valid")

deduped_df = (valid_df
    .withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(
        Window.partitionBy("order_id", "event_type").orderBy(F.col("ingested_at").desc())
    ))
    .filter("rn = 1")
    .drop("rn", "is_valid"))

deduped_df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save("/silver/order_events")
quarantine_df.write.format("delta").mode("append").save("/quarantine/order_events")
questions.modelAnswer: Bronze preserves raw, as-landed data exactly as ingested, duplicates and malformed rows included, specifically so nothing is ever lost and reprocessing from scratch is always possible if a downstream bug is found later. Silver is where real cleaning happens -- schema validation, deduplication, and type casting -- but rows failing validation are explicitly routed to a quarantine table rather than filtered out silently, because a silent drop makes a data quality problem invisible until someone eventually notices missing records downstream, while a quarantine table gives a concrete, queryable record of exactly what was rejected and why, enabling later investigation or reprocessing once the root cause is fixed upstream. The deduplication step uses row_number() over a window partitioned by the event's natural identity, keeping only the most recently ingested version per key -- a standard pattern for CDC-like or at-least-once delivery sources where the same logical event can legitimately arrive more than once. Gold (not shown here) builds further, business-level aggregation on top of this clean silver table; none of that aggregation logic belongs at this layer.
questions.professionalAnswer: The detail I'd defend most is the quarantine table rather than a plain filter -- I've seen 'just filter out the bad rows' quietly hide a real upstream data quality bug for weeks, because nobody notices records are missing until a report doesn't reconcile. Writing rejected rows somewhere queryable turns that into a visible, actionable signal instead. On deduplication, the ordering inside the window function matters more than it looks -- I always pick a genuinely deterministic tiebreaker, like the latest ingested_at, so the result is reproducible if the job is ever rerun against the same bronze data.

Deduplicating without a deterministic ordering/tiebreaker, making the result non-reproducible across reruns
Doing heavy business aggregation logic in silver instead of leaving that responsibility for gold
Using overwrite mode on silver without considering whether downstream consumers actually need incremental processing instead

Silver enforces schema, type casting, and deduplication, producing clean, validated data
Invalid rows are routed to a quarantine table, never silently dropped
Deduplication needs a deterministic ordering to produce reproducible results across reruns
Gold is reserved for business-level aggregation and modeling, not silver

Correctly implements deterministic deduplication via a window function

questions.title: Writing Bicep with @secure() Parameters and Child Resource Dependencies
questions.prompt: Write a Bicep template that provisions a SQL Server and a database as a child resource, passing the administrator password as a @secure() parameter, and explain how Bicep's nested/child resource syntax establishes the dependency automatically.
questions.modelAnswer: @secure() marks a parameter so its value is never shown in deployment logs, the Azure Activity Log, or Bicep/ARM deployment outputs -- it must be supplied at deploy time through a parameter file, a Key Vault reference, or a CI/CD secret, never hardcoded, and Azure masks it wherever it would otherwise be displayed. Declaring the database resource nested inside the sqlServer resource body is Bicep's child-resource syntax -- it automatically establishes both correct name scoping (the database's full resource name becomes server/database under the hood) and an implicit dependsOn relationship, guaranteeing the server is fully provisioned before the database resource is created, with no explicit dependsOn line required from the author at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: The password parameter marked @secure() is non-negotiable for anything like an admin login -- without it, that value would show up in deployment history and logs in plain text, which defeats the entire point of treating it as a secret. The nested database block is the other detail worth calling out: I didn't have to write dependsOn anywhere, because declaring it as a child resource inside sqlServer's body tells Bicep the relationship directly, and it compiles down to the correct dependency and name scoping automatically. I'd only reach for an explicit dependsOn when the relationship between two resources isn't a true parent-child one that nesting can express.

Giving a secure parameter a hardcoded default value, which still risks exposure through source control
Forgetting to add @allowed() restrictions on values like SKU tier where they should be constrained
keyPoints: @secure() prevents a parameter's value from appearing in logs or deployment outputs
Secrets should come from a parameter file, Key Vault, or CI secret store, never a hardcoded default

Implicit dependencies via nesting are preferable to manual dependsOn for genuine parent-child relationships
Explicit dependsOn is still appropriate when the relationship between resources isn't a true nested one

questions.title: Diagnosing Duplicate Rows in a dbt Incremental Model
questions.prompt: A dbt model materialized as incremental is producing duplicate rows after a backfill was run twice by mistake. Walk through how you'd diagnose the cause and what you'd check in the model's config.
questions.modelAnswer: First check the model's config block for unique_key and incremental_strategy -- the most common cause of this exact symptom is a model with materialized='incremental' but no unique_key set, which, depending on the adapter's default behavior, often falls back to a plain append strategy; re-running the same batch twice then simply inserts every row from that batch a second time with no deduplication at all. Second, even with unique_key configured, verify incremental_strategy is actually merge or delete+insert rather than append explicitly overriding the intended default, since some adapters require incremental_strategy to be set explicitly alongside unique_key rather than inferring it. Third, verify the unique_key itself is genuinely unique at the table's intended grain -- if it's a single column but the real grain needs a composite key (order_id alone when the table is really at order_id plus line_number grain), merge will either update the wrong row or still produce duplicates whenever multiple source rows legitimately map to the same key. The fix path: identify and remove the existing duplicates with a one-time cleanup query keyed on the correct grain, then correct the model's config, then re-run deliberately to confirm a repeated run no longer reintroduces duplicates.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start exactly where this kind of bug almost always lives: the config block. No unique_key, or a unique_key that doesn't actually match grain, explains the overwhelming majority of 'duplicates after a rerun' reports I've seen. I'd fix the config, then run a quick GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 check at the real grain before and after cleanup, both to confirm the existing duplicates are gone and that the fixed config doesn't quietly produce new ones on the next run.

Not verifying the unique_key actually matches the table's real grain, including composite keys
Fixing the config without first cleaning up the duplicates already sitting in the table
Not adding a dbt test afterward (like a uniqueness test on the correct grain) to catch this regressing silently in the future
keyPoints: Incremental materialization without unique_key often defaults to unsafe append behavior
unique_key must match the model's actual grain, including any composite keys
Existing duplicates must be manually cleaned up after fixing config, since the fix doesn't retroactively deduplicate
Add a uniqueness test at the correct grain after fixing this, to catch a regression automatically
Confirm the fix by rerunning the same batch deliberately and checking no new duplicates appear

questions.title: A DAG That Passes Locally but Fails Only in Production
questions.prompt: A DAG runs fine when tested locally with the Airflow CLI, but every production run fails at the same task with a connection timeout. Walk through your diagnostic process.
questions.modelAnswer: Identical code behaving differently between two environments almost always points to an environment or configuration difference, not a code bug, so the first check is Airflow Connections: does the production Airflow instance's connection ID actually point at the correct host and credentials, or has it drifted to a different, possibly firewalled or wrong-region endpoint compared to what local testing used? Next, check network reachability specifically from the production worker's own network context -- a managed Airflow environment's workers often sit in a different VNet/VPC/subnet than a local development machine, and a database or API reachable from a laptop (which may ride a VPN with broader access) can be entirely blocked by production's network security group or firewall rules. Also check whether the production connection uses a different authentication method than what was tested locally -- managed identity in production versus a connection string locally, for instance -- which can fail silently or with a misleading timeout rather than a clear authentication error. Finally, check for resource constraints: a production worker under real load might simply be slower to establish a connection than a quiet local environment, tipping over a timeout threshold that never gets approached locally.
questions.professionalAnswer: My instinct whenever the exact same code passes locally and fails only in production is to stop looking at the DAG file entirely and start comparing environments side by side. Connections is where I look first -- it's astonishingly common for a production connection to point somewhere subtly different than what was tested. After that, network path: production workers frequently live behind firewall rules a developer's laptop or VPN never has to deal with. I'd only go back to the code itself once I've ruled out connection config, network reachability, and auth method differences, because in my experience that's where this specific failure signature almost always resolves.

Not checking for Airflow Connections configuration differences between environments as the first step
Forgetting network security groups/firewalls differ between a local machine's network path and production workers' path
Not checking whether production's connection uses different authentication than what was tested locally

questions.title: Diagnosing a Sudden Spike in Consumer Lag on One Partition
questions.prompt: Consumer lag metrics show the overall topic lag is fine, but one specific partition out of twelve is accumulating lag continuously while the others stay near zero. What's your diagnosis, and how do you confirm it?
questions.modelAnswer: The symptom -- one partition's lag growing continuously while its siblings stay flat -- is the classic signature of a hot partition caused by skewed key distribution: if messages are keyed by something like customer_id or tenant_id and one key (or a small cluster of keys) accounts for a disproportionate share of total traffic, every message for that key lands on the same partition by design through consistent hashing, and the single consumer thread assigned to that partition becomes a bottleneck no matter how many total consumers or partitions exist elsewhere in the group. To confirm: check per-partition incoming message rates, not just lag, via consumer group describe output or broker metrics -- a genuinely hot partition shows a much higher incoming message rate than its siblings, not merely higher lag, which rules out the alternative explanation of simply slower per-message processing on that partition. Also check whether a specific message type or a slow downstream call (an external API lookup triggered only by that key's data) is compounding the skew with longer per-message processing time, which would show normal-ish volume but still accumulate lag. The fix depends on the actual root cause: for genuine key skew, consider a composite or salted key to spread that hot entity's traffic across multiple partitions, accepting a loss of strict per-entity ordering, or isolate that specific large tenant onto dedicated infrastructure; if it's slow per-message processing rather than volume, the fix belongs in the consumer's processing logic, not in repartitioning.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd check per-partition message rate before touching anything else, because lag alone doesn't tell you whether this partition is getting hammered with volume or just processing slowly -- those two root causes need completely different fixes. If the rate is genuinely higher on that one partition, that's skewed keying, and the fix is almost always about how messages get keyed, not about adding more consumers, since only one consumer is ever actively assigned to that single partition regardless of total consumer count. If the rate looks normal but lag still climbs, I'd look at what's different about processing that specific partition's messages -- often a slow downstream dependency only triggered by a particular kind of record.
commonMistakes: Assuming a lag spike is always a consumer-side bug without first checking per-partition incoming message rate
Adding more consumer instances as a fix, when a single hot partition's ceiling is set by its one assigned consumer, not total consumer count
Not distinguishing between unusually high message volume and unusually slow per-message processing as separate root causes
Applying a blanket repartitioning/salting fix without checking whether strict per-entity ordering actually matters downstream
keyPoints: A single hot partition while siblings stay flat typically points to skewed key distribution
More consumer instances don't help a single partition's bottleneck -- only one consumer is ever actively assigned to it
Per-partition message rate, not just lag, is needed to distinguish high volume from slow processing
Salting or composite keys trade strict per-entity ordering for better load distribution
Isolating a known large/hot entity onto dedicated infrastructure is a valid alternative to repartitioning

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses skewed key distribution as the likely cause
Correctly proposes checking per-partition message rate to confirm
Distinguishes high volume from slow processing as separate root causes
Proposes a valid fix matched to the actual root cause

questions.title: A Poison-Pill Message Is Breaking the Consumer's Retry Loop
questions.prompt: A consumer crashes repeatedly on the same offset -- it retries, fails on the same malformed message, retries again, and never advances, blocking every message behind it. Diagnose the problem and describe how you'd fix the pipeline so this can't happen again.
questions.modelAnswer: This is the classic poison-pill scenario: a single malformed or otherwise unprocessable message causes the consumer to throw an exception every time it's processed, and because the consumer never commits its offset past that message, a naive retry loop simply re-reads and re-fails on the exact same message indefinitely -- completely blocking every message behind it in that partition, with lag on that partition growing unbounded even though the broker and network are both perfectly healthy. Confirm this by checking consumer logs for the same exception recurring at the same offset repeatedly, and inspect that specific message's raw payload directly, for example by seeking a console consumer to that exact offset, to find the actual malformation -- a schema mismatch, an unexpected null, a field that fails parsing. The structural fix is to never let a single message's processing failure block the pipeline unboundedly: wrap message processing in a try/except at the per-message level, not per-batch, and route any message that fails after a bounded number of retries with backoff (reserved for genuinely transient failures) to a dead-letter queue topic instead of blocking further -- the consumer commits past the bad message and keeps moving, while the DLQ preserves the bad message for later inspection and reprocessing once the root cause is understood.
questions.professionalAnswer: The giveaway here is lag climbing on exactly one partition while the consumer's own logs show the identical exception at the identical offset over and over -- that's not a transient issue that retrying will eventually get past, it's a message that will never successfully process no matter how many times it's retried. The actual fix is architectural, not a retry-count tweak: processing needs a bounded retry count for genuinely transient failures, and anything that still fails after that needs to go to a dead-letter topic so the consumer can commit past it and keep the rest of the partition moving, rather than sitting there indefinitely.
commonMistakes: Retrying indefinitely with no cap, assuming the message will somehow become processable on a later attempt
Not distinguishing transient failures (worth retrying with backoff) from permanently malformed messages (never worth retrying)
Committing offsets at batch granularity without understanding exactly which message within the batch is failing
Building a DLQ without enough metadata captured to actually triage why messages ended up there later
keyPoints: A poison-pill message blocks everything behind it when the consumer can't advance past a failing offset
Confirm by checking for the same exception/offset repeating in consumer logs
Route permanently failing messages to a DLQ after bounded retries rather than retrying forever
Transient failures should be retried with backoff; permanently malformed messages should be quarantined immediately
The consumer must commit past the bad message once it's routed to the DLQ, so the rest of the partition keeps moving

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the poison-pill mechanism blocking the partition
Correctly describes confirming via repeated exception/offset in logs
Correctly proposes a DLQ with bounded retries as the structural fix
Distinguishes transient vs. permanent failure handling

questions.title: Diagnosing an Unexpected 'Destroy and Recreate' in Terraform Plan
questions.prompt: You run terraform plan expecting a small, additive change, but the output shows an existing production database resource will be destroyed and recreated. Walk through how you'd diagnose why, and what you'd check before anyone runs apply.
questions.modelAnswer: First, read the plan output carefully for exactly which attribute is marked as forcing replacement -- Terraform explicitly annotates attributes that require a destroy/recreate rather than an in-place update, usually noting something like 'forces replacement' right next to the specific changed attribute. Many resource arguments are immutable after creation for a given cloud provider, and changing even something that looks minor in config, like a storage engine setting or an instance's configuration parameter group in certain configurations, can force a full replace rather than an update. Second, check whether the deployed resource has actually drifted from what's recorded in state -- if someone changed the resource manually in the cloud console since the last apply, the plan's diff is comparing your config against its last-known state, not necessarily today's real-world resource, and a refresh might reveal the 'change' is really reconciling drift rather than reflecting the edit you intended to make. Third, check whether a recent provider version upgrade changed how an attribute is represented internally, a known source of spurious diffs that can look like a destructive change when it's actually just a schema-representation change in the provider itself. Before anyone runs apply: get explicit confirmation on which exact attribute is forcing replacement, confirm whether destroying this specific resource causes real data loss (a database almost always does), and if the change is genuinely intentional, verify there's a backup/migration plan in place first -- never apply a destroy/recreate on a stateful production resource without that confirmation.
questions.professionalAnswer: Reading plan output line by line, specifically for the words next to a forced replacement, is the whole first step -- I've seen people skip straight past that annotation and only notice the destroy/recreate when the summary line at the bottom says '1 to destroy, 1 to add.' After identifying the specific attribute, I check whether this is really an intended config change or whether someone touched the resource manually in the console since the last apply, since that drift can masquerade as something the plan 'needs to fix.' For anything stateful like a database, I treat a destroy/recreate as a hard stop until there's an explicit, confirmed plan for the data, not just an acknowledgment that the plan looks scary.
commonMistakes: Running apply without reading exactly which attribute triggered the forced replacement
Not checking for manual, out-of-band changes in the cloud console that could be causing apparent drift
Assuming a provider version bump never introduces spurious diff behavior
Applying a destructive plan against a stateful production resource without confirming the data-loss impact first
keyPoints: Terraform annotates exactly which attribute forces replacement -- always read it before applying
Manual out-of-band changes in the cloud console can masquerade as an intended destructive diff
A provider version upgrade can introduce spurious diffs unrelated to any real config change
Never apply a destroy/recreate against a stateful production resource without confirming data-loss impact
A backup or migration plan should exist before applying any confirmed, intentional destructive change

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies reading the forces-replacement annotation as the first step
Correctly considers drift from manual out-of-band changes as a cause
Correctly considers a provider version upgrade as a possible spurious-diff cause
Correctly insists on confirming data-loss impact before ever applying

questions.title: A Secret Was Committed and Merged — Why a .gitignore Fix Isn't Enough
questions.prompt: A PR accidentally committed a real database password to a config file, and it was merged to main before anyone noticed. A later PR added that file to .gitignore and removed it from the current working tree. Explain why the secret is still exposed, and what actually needs to happen.
questions.modelAnswer: Adding a file to .gitignore and deleting it in a later commit only stops it from being tracked going forward -- it does nothing whatsoever to the repository's history, where the original commit containing the real secret still exists, fully readable by anyone who clones the repo, checks out that earlier commit, or simply runs git log -p or git show against that specific commit hash. Removing the file going forward is necessary but addresses essentially none of the actual exposure, because the full file content at that historical commit is permanently retrievable as long as that commit remains in the repository's object history, and on a hosted platform even a later force-pushed history rewrite doesn't guarantee removal from cached forks, CI run logs, or the platform's own caches without an explicit support request for a genuinely sensitive leak. Two things actually need to happen: first and most urgently, treat the credential itself as compromised and rotate it immediately -- change the real database password, revoke the old one -- because that is the only fix that's guaranteed regardless of what happens to the git history afterward. Second, if the history itself needs to be cleaned, for compliance reasons or simply to stop it appearing in future clones, rewrite history with a tool like git filter-repo or BFG Repo-Cleaner to strip the secret from every commit that ever contained it, force-push the rewritten history, and have every collaborator re-clone or hard-reset their local copies, since their existing local commits now point to objects that no longer exist on the remote.
questions.professionalAnswer: The .gitignore fix feels like it closed the issue, but it genuinely didn't touch the actual exposure at all -- that original commit, with the real password sitting in it, is still sitting in the repository's history, retrievable with a one-line git command by anyone with clone access. Rotating the credential is the step I'd insist happens immediately, independent of anything else, because it's the only guarantee that matters regardless of what the git history ends up looking like. Cleaning the history with filter-repo or BFG is worth doing too, mainly to stop the leaked value from continuing to show up in future clones or audits, but I'd never treat that as a substitute for rotation, and I'd make sure the whole team knows a rewritten history means everyone needs to re-sync their local copies.
commonMistakes: Believing a later commit that deletes the file also removes it from the repository's history
Treating .gitignore as retroactive protection rather than a forward-only tracking rule
Skipping credential rotation because 'we cleaned the history,' when rotation is the only guaranteed fix regardless of git state
Rewriting history without warning the team, breaking everyone's existing local branches and clones
keyPoints: Deleting a file in a later commit leaves the secret fully recoverable in earlier commits' history
Rotating the actual credential is the only guaranteed fix, independent of git history
History rewriting (filter-repo or BFG) plus a force-push is needed if the history itself must be scrubbed
Every collaborator must re-sync after a history rewrite, since old commit hashes become invalid
Even a force-pushed rewrite may not remove the secret from cached forks or CI logs without further action

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why deleting the file doesn't remove it from history
Correctly identifies credential rotation as the only guaranteed fix
Correctly describes history rewriting as the remediation for the history itself
Mentions the team-wide re-sync consequence of a force-pushed history rewrite

questions.title: Diagnosing a Failed Job After Running OPTIMIZE and VACUUM Concurrently
questions.prompt: A streaming MERGE job into a Delta table started failing with a concurrent modification error right after a scheduled OPTIMIZE job kicked off on the same table. Separately, a long-running batch read job failed with a 'file not found' error after VACUUM ran. Explain both failures.
questions.modelAnswer: The MERGE-vs-OPTIMIZE conflict: OPTIMIZE compacts small files into larger ones, which is itself a write operation that creates a new commit in the transaction log; if a concurrent MERGE is also trying to commit changes that touch files OPTIMIZE just rewrote, or vice versa, Delta's optimistic concurrency control detects that overlap at commit time and fails one of the two transactions with a concurrent modification exception -- this isn't a bug, it's the protection mechanism working exactly as designed, but it does mean MERGE and OPTIMIZE contending for the same table at the same time will periodically produce a transaction that must retry. The VACUUM-vs-long-running-read failure is a different mechanism entirely: VACUUM physically deletes data files no longer referenced by the current table version and older than the configured retention threshold, 7 days by default; if a long-running read job began its read against an older table snapshot, or a Time Travel query, whose files are exactly the ones VACUUM just deleted, the read fails with file-not-found because the files it needs no longer physically exist anywhere. The fix for the first: schedule OPTIMIZE during lower-write windows, or ensure the pipeline retries on concurrent-modification exceptions, which Delta exceptions are specifically designed to be retried against, since a retry simply reads the newly-committed state. The fix for the second: raise VACUUM's retention threshold to cover the longest-running read or Time Travel query the pipeline needs to support, or coordinate VACUUM's schedule to avoid windows when long-running historical reads are active.
questions.professionalAnswer: These two failures look similar on the surface -- both involve maintenance jobs breaking something else -- but they're actually different mechanisms and need different fixes. The OPTIMIZE-vs-MERGE collision is a legitimate concurrent-modification exception, and the right response is to retry the losing transaction, not to treat it as a bug to suppress; I'd also look at just not scheduling OPTIMIZE during the pipeline's busiest write windows if it's happening often enough to matter. The VACUUM failure is more serious because it's irreversible -- once VACUUM deletes files past the retention threshold, there's no undo, so the actual fix is making sure that threshold is set with the longest-running read or Time Travel use case in mind before VACUUM ever runs again.
commonMistakes: Treating a concurrent modification exception as a bug to suppress rather than a signal to retry the transaction
Running VACUUM with an aggressively low retention period without considering long-running jobs or Time Travel queries that depend on older files
Scheduling OPTIMIZE and heavy concurrent write jobs at the same time with no retry logic in the pipeline
Not understanding VACUUM is irreversible once eligible files are physically deleted -- there's no undo
keyPoints: OPTIMIZE is itself a write operation and can trigger legitimate concurrent-modification conflicts with concurrent writers
A concurrent-modification exception should be retried, not suppressed or treated as a bug
VACUUM physically deletes old files past the retention threshold, which can break long-running reads or Time Travel queries referencing them
Retention threshold should be set based on the longest-running query or job that might need historical files
VACUUM's file deletion is irreversible once it executes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the OPTIMIZE/MERGE concurrent-modification mechanism
Correctly explains the VACUUM/long-running-read file-not-found mechanism
Proposes a correct fix for the OPTIMIZE/MERGE conflict (scheduling or retry)
Proposes a correct fix for the VACUUM issue (retention threshold tuning)

questions.title: Diagnosing a Fabric Semantic Model That Silently Degrades from Direct Lake to DirectQuery
questions.prompt: A Power BI report built on a Fabric Direct Lake semantic model was fast, then suddenly got much slower with no code change. Walk through what could cause Direct Lake to fall back to a slower query mode, and how you'd confirm that's what happened.
questions.modelAnswer: Direct Lake mode reads Delta Parquet files directly into memory without a separate import or refresh step, which is what gives it near-import-mode speed without the staleness of a scheduled refresh -- but it relies on specific conditions to stay on that fast path. A common cause of silent degradation is the underlying Delta table accumulating too many small files or row groups without regular OPTIMIZE/VACUUM maintenance, which increases the cost of the in-memory transcoding Direct Lake performs on read; another is the table exceeding size or row-group guardrails that trigger Fabric's automatic fallback to DirectQuery, querying the lakehouse or warehouse directly per visual instead of reading in-memory, specifically to protect overall capacity health once those thresholds are crossed. A third cause is specific DAX patterns or model features -- certain complex relationships, calculated columns, or functions -- that Direct Lake doesn't support natively, forcing a fallback for just those particular queries rather than the whole model. To confirm: check the workspace's capacity metrics app or the semantic model's query diagnostics, which explicitly surface whether a given query ran in Direct Lake or fell back to DirectQuery, and check the underlying Delta table's file and row-group statistics for signs of fragmentation that would warrant a maintenance job.
questions.professionalAnswer: When a Direct Lake report slows down with literally no report or model change, I go straight to the underlying Delta tables' maintenance history before touching anything in Power BI itself -- fragmented, un-optimized files are a very common, very invisible cause, since nobody 'changed' anything from the report author's point of view. I'd also check Fabric's own diagnostics for an explicit fallback signal, because guessing whether it's actually hitting Direct Lake or has silently fallen back to DirectQuery is the kind of thing that should be confirmed with real data, not assumed from the symptom alone.
commonMistakes: Assuming Direct Lake mode is permanent and immune to fallback once configured
Not running regular table maintenance (OPTIMIZE) on the Delta tables feeding the semantic model
Not checking Fabric's own diagnostics/capacity metrics for an explicit fallback signal before guessing at the cause
Assuming any slowdown must be a DAX or report-design problem without first ruling out the storage-layer cause
keyPoints: Direct Lake reads Delta Parquet directly into memory for near-import speed without a scheduled refresh
File/row-group fragmentation from lack of maintenance increases in-memory transcoding cost
Size or row-group guardrails can trigger an automatic fallback to the slower DirectQuery path
Certain DAX patterns aren't supported in Direct Lake and force a per-query fallback
Fabric's capacity metrics and query diagnostics explicitly show whether a fallback actually occurred

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains Direct Lake's in-memory read mechanism
Correctly identifies fragmentation/maintenance as a cause of fallback
Correctly identifies unsupported DAX patterns as a per-query fallback cause
Correctly describes confirming fallback via Fabric's own diagnostics

questions.title: Using Query Profile to Diagnose an Unexpected Full Table Scan
questions.prompt: A query filtering on a timestamp column that you expected to prune well is taking far longer than expected. Walk through how you'd use Snowflake's Query Profile to confirm it's doing a full table scan, and what you'd check to fix it.
questions.code:
-- Bad: wrapping the column defeats pruning
-- WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2026-01-01'

-- Good: direct range predicate on the raw column
SELECT *
FROM events
WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-01-02';
questions.modelAnswer: Open Query Profile for the completed query and check the TableScan operator's statistics, specifically 'Partitions scanned' against 'Partitions total' -- if those two numbers are equal, or nearly so, Snowflake pruned essentially nothing and scanned the whole table, confirming the suspicion directly rather than guessing from run time alone. The most common cause when filtering on a column expected to prune well is that the filter predicate doesn't align with how Snowflake's micro-partition metadata (min/max values per partition) was actually built -- often because the table's natural ingestion order doesn't correlate with the filtered column, so rows for a given date range end up scattered across many micro-partitions rather than landing together, and every partition's stored min/max range ends up overlapping the filter, leaving nothing to prune. Another very common cause is wrapping the filtered column in a function, such as DATE(created_at) = '2026-01-01' instead of a direct range predicate on created_at itself -- wrapping a column defeats pruning because Snowflake generally can't match a transformed expression against the raw stored min/max metadata. The fix: rewrite the filter as a direct range predicate on the raw column, and if clustering truly doesn't align with query patterns, consider an explicit clustering key on that column, understanding the ongoing reclustering cost that comes with it, or restructure ingestion so new data naturally clusters along the dimension most commonly filtered.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always pull up Query Profile and look at partitions scanned versus partitions total before assuming anything about why a query is slow -- that single comparison tells you immediately whether pruning happened at all. The fix I see needed most often is rewriting a filter that wraps the column in a function into a plain range predicate instead, since that one change alone restores pruning without touching the table's physical layout at all. Only if pruning is still poor after that would I look at a clustering key, and even then I'd weigh its ongoing reclustering cost against the actual query-performance gain before adding one.
commonMistakes: Not checking partitions scanned vs. partitions total in Query Profile before guessing at a fix
Wrapping the filtered column in a function, unknowingly defeating partition pruning
Assuming a clustering key is always worth adding, without weighing its ongoing maintenance/reclustering cost
Blaming warehouse size for slowness instead of first checking whether pruning happened at all
keyPoints: Query Profile's partitions scanned vs. partitions total directly confirms whether pruning occurred
Pruning depends on micro-partition min/max metadata aligning with the filter, which depends on ingestion/clustering order
Wrapping a filtered column in a function typically defeats pruning against the stored metadata
A direct range predicate on the raw column is usually the first and simplest fix
A clustering key can help further but carries an ongoing reclustering cost worth weighing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains using partitions scanned vs. total to confirm a full scan
Correctly identifies ingestion-order/clustering misalignment as a root cause
Correctly identifies function-wrapped predicates as defeating pruning
Proposes correct, prioritized fixes (rewrite filter first, clustering key as a further option)

questions.title: Diagnosing Stale Slim CI Results from state:modified+
questions.prompt: Your dbt Slim CI job is supposed to only build models that changed in a PR plus their downstream dependents, but it's building almost the entire DAG on every PR, defeating the purpose. Diagnose what's misconfigured.
questions.modelAnswer: dbt build --select state:modified+ compares the current project's manifest against a previously stored production-state manifest to determine which models genuinely changed; if nearly everything is flagged as modified, the most likely cause is that the comparison manifest passed via --state isn't an accurate, fresh snapshot of production -- either it's stale, pointing at a manifest from weeks ago before many unrelated changes already landed on main, or the deferral/state artifact simply isn't being generated and stored correctly after every successful main-branch run, so CI ends up comparing against an out-of-date or entirely wrong baseline. Another common cause: state comparison is sensitive to anything that changes a model's compiled SQL, including changes that aren't that model's own business logic -- a shared macro, a project variable, or an env_var default referenced across many models can cause state:modified+ to flag every model using it, even though their individual intended logic didn't change at all, which can look exactly like 'nearly everything changed' when really one widely-used macro changed. The fix: confirm the CI pipeline has a step that uploads and stores manifest.json from every successful main-branch run to a location the PR's CI job can reliably retrieve as --state, and separately audit any PR touching shared macros/variables for a legitimately wide blast radius versus an accidentally over-broad diff.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd check is whether the production manifest being passed as --state is actually current -- stale or missing manifests are the single most common cause of this exact symptom, and it's an easy thing to silently break if the step that persists manifest.json after a main-branch run gets removed or starts failing quietly. If the manifest is confirmed fresh and the problem persists, I'd look at whether the PR touched something widely shared, like a core macro -- that's not a bug, that's state:modified+ correctly identifying a broad blast radius, even though it feels like something is wrong.
commonMistakes: Not automatically persisting and updating the production manifest after every successful main-branch deploy, leaving PR comparisons against a stale baseline
Forgetting that touching a widely-shared macro or variable legitimately marks many dependent models as modified
Using --defer without --state pointed at the correct, current manifest, silently breaking the whole mechanism
Not realizing seed or full-refresh changes can have different state-comparison behavior than ordinary model changes
keyPoints: state:modified+ compares against a stored production manifest, and a stale or missing manifest breaks the whole optimization
The production manifest must be regenerated and stored after every successful main-branch run
A change to a shared macro or variable legitimately flags everything downstream of it, which can look broken but isn't
--defer requires the same accurate --state to resolve unbuilt upstream references correctly
Confirm manifest freshness before assuming the broad build is a bug rather than a correct wide blast radius

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies a stale/missing production manifest as the likely root cause
Correctly explains shared macro/variable changes legitimately widening the diff
Correctly explains the role of --defer and --state together
Proposes a correct fix (persisting manifest.json after every main-branch run)

questions.title: A Fleet of Sensors in Poke Mode Is Exhausting Worker Slots
questions.prompt: Several DAGs use sensors waiting on files that can take hours to arrive, each sensor set to poke mode. The Airflow deployment starts failing to schedule new tasks because all worker slots are occupied. Diagnose the cause and the fix.
questions.modelAnswer: Poke mode keeps a sensor's worker slot continuously occupied for the sensor's entire waiting period -- the task is in a running state the whole time, even though it's doing nothing but checking a condition every poke_interval and sleeping in between; with sensors that can wait for hours, each one ties up a full worker slot for that entire duration, and enough concurrent long-waiting sensors can exhaust the available worker pool entirely, starving every other task in the deployment, including completely unrelated DAGs, from ever being scheduled, since there's simply nowhere left to run them. Confirm by checking scheduler and worker metrics for slot saturation that correlates directly with the number of concurrently running poke-mode sensor tasks at that time. The fix is switching these sensors to reschedule mode, which releases the worker slot entirely between poke intervals -- the sensor's task instance moves to an up_for_reschedule state rather than holding a slot while it waits, freeing that slot to serve other tasks in the meantime, with the sensor simply getting rescheduled to check again at the next interval. Reschedule mode is specifically designed for this exact situation: long, unpredictable wait times where constant occupancy of a worker slot isn't actually needed.
questions.professionalAnswer: The symptom to recognize here is that it's not any one DAG failing -- it's the whole deployment failing to schedule anything new, which is a strong signal of resource exhaustion rather than a bug in a specific DAG's logic. Once I see several long-waiting sensors all in poke mode, that's almost certainly the cause: each one is holding a worker slot hostage for hours doing nothing but occasionally checking a condition. Switching them to reschedule mode is close to a free fix for this exact pattern -- it releases the slot between checks instead of holding it the whole time, and it's specifically what reschedule mode exists for.
commonMistakes: Defaulting every sensor to poke mode without considering expected wait duration
Not recognizing that a worker-slot exhaustion symptom affecting unrelated DAGs points to resource contention, not a bug in any specific DAG
Using reschedule mode's default poke_interval without tuning it for genuinely long waits, adding unnecessary scheduler overhead
Not considering deferrable operators/triggers as an even lighter-weight alternative to reschedule mode for very long waits
keyPoints: Poke mode holds a full worker slot for the sensor's entire wait duration
Many concurrent long-waiting poke sensors can exhaust the worker pool and starve unrelated DAGs
A deployment-wide scheduling failure (not one DAG) signals resource contention rather than a code bug
Reschedule mode releases the slot between checks, suited to long/unpredictable waits
Deferrable operators are an even lighter-weight alternative where available in newer Airflow versions

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains poke mode's continuous slot occupation
Correctly diagnoses deployment-wide scheduling failure as resource exhaustion
Correctly proposes reschedule mode as the fix and explains why it works
Mentions deferrable operators as a further alternative

questions.title: A Correct dbt Mart Is Producing Numbers That Disagree with Another Report
questions.prompt: Finance says your revenue mart's total is higher than their source system's total for the same period, even though every individual model passed its tests and the SQL looks correct. Walk through how you'd diagnose this.
questions.code:
-- Test uniqueness on the join key BEFORE it's used in a join
SELECT customer_key, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM dim_customer
WHERE is_current = 1
GROUP BY customer_key
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
questions.modelAnswer: When every model's own logic and tests pass but an aggregate number still comes out inflated, the most common root cause is join fanout: a join between two tables where the real relationship is actually one-to-many or many-to-many rather than the one-to-one the query implicitly assumes, which duplicates a row from the 'one' side once per matching row on the 'many' side before any aggregation happens, so SUM(revenue) ends up summing the same revenue value multiple times, once per duplicate. This passes individual model tests because each model's own grain and uniqueness tests, if they exist, check that model in isolation, not the downstream join's actual cardinality -- the inflation is introduced specifically at the join itself, often inside the mart or even inside a BI tool's own join, not within any single upstream model. To diagnose: check row counts before and after each join in the mart's lineage against what a genuine one-to-one relationship should produce; if a dimension table has multiple active rows per key, such as an SCD2 dimension with more than one is_current = 1 row due to a data quality bug, or if the join key simply isn't actually unique on the dimension side, that join is silently duplicating fact rows. The fix: add a test asserting uniqueness on the dimension side of every join key before it's ever used in a join, not just after the whole mart is built, and audit for any place a one-to-many relationship was assumed to be one-to-one.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move when numbers don't reconcile despite every test passing is to stop trusting that passing tests rules out fanout, because fanout is specifically a join-time problem, not something a single model's own tests would ever catch. I'd check whether any dimension involved in the mart's joins could have more than one row per key -- an SCD2 dimension with a duplicate is_current row is the single most common source I've actually run into -- and I'd test uniqueness on exactly the column used as the join key, before the join, not after the mart is already built and the damage is done.
commonMistakes: Assuming passing model-level tests rules out a join-fanout problem downstream, when fanout is a join-time issue, not a single-model issue
Only testing uniqueness after the final mart is built, rather than on the join key itself before joining
Not checking for duplicate 'current' rows in an SCD2 dimension as a specific, common fanout source
Fixing the symptom (deduplicating or dividing late in the query) instead of the actual root cause, the join cardinality itself
keyPoints: Join fanout duplicates fact rows when a join's real cardinality is one-to-many but was assumed one-to-one
Fanout inflates any SUM/COUNT computed after the join, without any individual model test catching it
A classic source of fanout is an SCD2 dimension accidentally having more than one current row per key
Fix by testing join-key uniqueness before the join happens, not just auditing the final mart output
Row-count checks before and after each join in the lineage help pinpoint exactly where the fanout is introduced

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses join fanout as the likely root cause
Correctly explains why individual model tests don't catch this
Correctly identifies a concrete common source (duplicate SCD2 current rows)
Proposes the correct fix (pre-join uniqueness testing on the join key)

questions.title: Designing a Medallion Pipeline for a Single Orders Data Source
questions.prompt: Design a bronze/silver/gold medallion pipeline for a single source: an operational orders system that emits CDC changes via Kafka. Walk through what lives in each layer, what transformations happen at each boundary, and how you'd handle schema evolution from the source.
questions.modelAnswer: Bronze ingests the raw CDC events from Kafka essentially as-is -- append-only, landing every change event (insert, update, delete) with its original payload plus a few audit columns (ingestion timestamp, source offset), using schema evolution/merge-schema settings so a new column the source starts emitting doesn't break ingestion. Nothing is deduplicated, validated, or reshaped here; the goal is a faithful, fully replayable record of everything that arrived, so any downstream bug can be fixed later by reprocessing from bronze rather than re-pulling from the source system, which may not retain history nearly as long. Silver applies the real transformation: deduplicating CDC events (keeping the latest version per primary key, or applying them in order via MERGE to materialize current-state tables), enforcing a stable, validated schema (casting types, routing non-conforming rows to quarantine rather than dropping them silently), and resolving the CDC log into a clean, queryable current-state orders table, plus optionally a historical table if past order states matter downstream. Gold builds business-level, aggregated marts on top of silver -- daily revenue by region, fulfillment SLAs -- denormalized and modeled specifically for how BI tools and analysts will actually query it, typically as a star schema. For schema evolution: bronze should tolerate new source columns without failing, silver should have an explicit, versioned schema contract that deliberately decides which new source columns get surfaced and how rather than passing every raw change straight through automatically, and any source column type change or removal should trigger a deliberate silver-layer migration rather than being silently absorbed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through the layers in terms of what responsibility each one owns, because that's really the design decision, not the storage tiering. Bronze's only job is fidelity -- capture everything exactly as it arrived, tolerate whatever schema drift the source throws at it, never lose anything. Silver's job is trust -- turn that raw, possibly messy CDC stream into something validated and deduplicated that the rest of the business can actually rely on, with a quarantine path for anything that doesn't conform rather than a silent drop. Gold's job is usefulness -- shape that trusted data into whatever specific, denormalized form the actual reporting needs. On schema evolution specifically, I'd be deliberate that bronze absorbing a new column automatically is fine and desirable, but letting that same new column silently flow all the way into silver without anyone deciding how it should be typed, named, or surfaced is exactly the kind of thing that causes confusing downstream surprises.
commonMistakes: Doing real business logic/aggregation in silver instead of leaving transformation-only work there and pushing aggregation to gold
Letting bronze's automatic schema evolution flow straight through to silver without a deliberate, reviewed mapping
Not building a quarantine path for malformed CDC events in silver, silently dropping them instead
Treating medallion layers as a storage-tiering decision rather than a transformation-responsibility boundary
keyPoints: Bronze preserves raw, replayable CDC events with tolerant schema evolution and zero transformation
Silver resolves CDC into a clean, validated, deduplicated current-state (and optionally historical) table
Gold is for business-level, query-optimized aggregation and modeling, not for cleaning or deduplication
Schema changes from the source should be deliberately reviewed before flowing past bronze, not silently passed through
A quarantine path in silver preserves visibility into malformed events instead of silently dropping them

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines bronze's raw, tolerant, replayable role
Correctly defines silver's validation/dedup/current-state role
Correctly defines gold's business-aggregation role, distinct from silver
Correctly describes a deliberate schema-evolution policy between layers

deepDive.heading: Handling deletes from CDC
deepDive.content: A delete event in CDC needs explicit handling in silver -- either a soft-delete flag (is_deleted = true, preserving the row for audit or history purposes) or a hard delete via MERGE's WHEN MATCHED ... THEN DELETE, depending on whether downstream consumers need to know something was removed or simply need it gone from the current-state view entirely.

deepDive.heading: Replay and reprocessing
deepDive.content: Because bronze is the durable, raw record, a bug discovered in silver's transformation logic can be fixed by re-running the bronze-to-silver job against the full bronze history, rather than needing to re-extract from the source system, which may have already aged out the relevant data from its own retention window. This is the core operational payoff of the medallion separation, and it's worth being explicit about in an interview because it's the actual reason the extra storage layer is worth its cost.

questions.title: Designing an Orchestrated dbt + Airflow Pipeline for Daily Incremental Loads
questions.prompt: Design an Airflow DAG that orchestrates a full daily pipeline: wait for a source file to land, load it into the warehouse, run dbt incremental models, run dbt tests, and only then refresh a downstream BI extract. What does the DAG structure look like, and where do failures get handled?
questions.modelAnswer: The DAG starts with a sensor, in reschedule mode since the file's arrival time is unpredictable and could be hours out, waiting on the source file landing in object storage, followed by a load task (a bulk-load operator or a COPY INTO-style statement) bringing the raw file into a staging or raw table. Next, a dbt build step, not separate run and test commands, runs the incremental models and their tests together, via BashOperator or a dedicated dbt-Airflow provider task group, so a failing test on one model blocks that model's downstream dependents from building on top of already-known-bad data within the same invocation, rather than letting bad data propagate further before anyone notices. Only after dbt build succeeds does a final task trigger the BI extract or semantic model refresh -- gating it behind dbt's success is the whole point of this ordering, since refreshing a BI layer on top of partially-built or test-failing data would surface wrong numbers directly to business users. Failure handling: the sensor needs a reasonable timeout with an alert if the file never arrives at all; the load and dbt tasks should have retries with backoff for transient infrastructure failures, like a flaky warehouse connection, but not for genuine data-quality test failures, which should fail fast and alert rather than retry blindly and delay the signal that something real is wrong. An on_failure_callback on the dbt task, which only fires after retries exhaust, should notify the data team with enough context (which model, which test) to act quickly, and the BI refresh task should never run at all if any upstream task failed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think about this DAG as having exactly one real gate: nothing downstream of dbt build should ever run unless dbt build genuinely succeeded, tests included. Everything else is in service of getting cleanly to that gate. The sensor in reschedule mode handles the unpredictable wait without tying up a worker slot the whole time. dbt build, not run-then-test, means a failing test actually stops bad data from propagating further within that same run, instead of just getting flagged after the fact. And I'm deliberate about which failures get automatic retries -- infrastructure blips, yes; a failed data-quality test, no, because retrying that just delays someone finding out something is actually wrong with the data.
commonMistakes: Using a poke-mode sensor for a file that could take hours to arrive, wasting a worker slot the whole time
Running dbt run and dbt test as separate tasks instead of dbt build, letting bad data flow downstream before tests catch it
Refreshing the BI extract unconditionally regardless of upstream success, surfacing wrong numbers to business users
Retrying data-quality test failures with the same backoff logic meant for transient infrastructure failures, delaying the alert
keyPoints: Use a reschedule-mode sensor for long, unpredictable file-arrival waits
dbt build interleaves run/test so failures block downstream models within the same run
The BI refresh must be explicitly gated behind dbt build's success, never run unconditionally
Distinguish retryable transient infrastructure failures from data-quality failures that should fail fast and alert
on_failure_callback should fire with enough context (model, test) for the team to act quickly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly structures the sensor-load-build-refresh DAG sequence
Correctly explains why dbt build is used over separate run/test
Correctly gates the BI refresh behind dbt build's success
Correctly distinguishes retryable vs. fail-fast failure handling

questions.title: Designing a CDC Ingestion Pipeline from an OLTP Database into a Lakehouse
questions.prompt: Design a pipeline that captures changes from a PostgreSQL OLTP database and lands them continuously in a lakehouse bronze layer, using Kafka Connect/Debezium-style CDC. Walk through the components and what happens to schema changes on the source.
questions.modelAnswer: A Debezium-style source connector reads PostgreSQL's write-ahead log via logical replication, rather than polling the tables directly, capturing every insert, update, and delete as a structured change event -- before/after images, operation type, source transaction metadata -- and publishing each table's changes to its own dedicated Kafka topic. A sink connector, or a Spark/Structured Streaming job consuming those topics directly, writes these events append-only into bronze Delta or Parquet tables, one per source table, preserving every change event exactly as captured; this bronze layer becomes a durable, replayable CDC log independent of how long the source database's own WAL happens to retain that history. From there, a silver-layer job, either batch or streaming using foreachBatch plus MERGE, resolves the CDC stream per table into a current-state table, applying inserts and updates in order and honoring deletes explicitly, whether as soft or hard deletes. For schema changes on the source: Debezium emits schema-change events alongside data events when integrated with a Schema Registry, and the registry's configured compatibility mode governs what kind of source schema change is absorbed safely and automatically, such as a new nullable column, versus what requires a deliberate update to the silver-layer mapping before it's surfaced further downstream, such as a column type change or removal.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe the WAL-based capture as the key design choice up front, because it's what makes this fundamentally different from a polling-based CDC approach -- Debezium reads the database's own replication stream rather than repeatedly querying tables for changes, which means it captures every change, including ones that happen and get overwritten between poll intervals, with much lower load on the source database. From there, bronze's job is just to be a faithful, replayable log of that CDC stream per table, and silver's job is resolving it into something queryable as current state. On schema evolution, I'd be specific that Debezium plus Schema Registry gives you an explicit signal when the source schema changes, and the compatibility mode is what decides whether that's something the pipeline absorbs automatically or something that needs a human to update the silver mapping first.
commonMistakes: Having the sink connector/job write only the latest state directly into a mutable table, losing the CDC audit trail bronze is supposed to preserve
Not registering Debezium's schema registry integration, leaving schema evolution entirely unmanaged
Assuming CDC captures every historical row rather than only changes from when the connector was started (an initial snapshot is a separate step)
Ignoring transaction boundaries, which matters if downstream logic needs to respect multi-table atomic changes from the source
keyPoints: Debezium-style CDC reads the database's write-ahead log rather than polling, capturing before/after images per change
Bronze preserves the raw CDC event stream per table as a durable, replayable log, independent of the source's own WAL retention
Silver resolves the CDC stream into current-state tables via MERGE, handling deletes explicitly
Schema registry compatibility mode governs which source schema changes are safely automatic vs. requiring a deliberate update
An initial snapshot is a separate, explicit step from ongoing CDC capture, needed to seed historical data
